executive_summary:
Rocket.Chat 9.1.0-develop (commit `9f3d6c8c4891`, Community edition, no licence, not Cloud-registered) was audited against the lab's documented secure baseline: the vendor's release image for the audited commit behind Traefik, MongoDB as a replica set, SMTP pointed at Mailpit, every security control at its shipped value (2FA, password policy, failed-login blocking, REST rate limiter, CSP, protected files), and Omnichannel, OAuth, SAML, CAS and anonymous read off. This is the expanded report: 84 ids, 73 of them real findings (1 critical, 10 high, 58 medium, 4 low by CVSS 3.1 band), each with its own `findings/VULN-NNN.md` carrying a 5 to 15 line excerpt copied from the target by line range, a description that says what the code does and what it should do, numbered reproduction steps against this lab's base URL and credentials, the CVSS vector metric by metric, and a fix with its side effects named as either removing a feature or removing only the weakness. The 11 filtered or documented entries sit in the trailing table with their reason and have no writeup, by design. 41 real findings need a non-default business feature and are listed under Edge cases: they are real for every deployment that turned that feature on, which for Omnichannel, OAuth or SAML is most of them.

What was not found matters as much: no unauthenticated remote code execution, no SQL or command injection, no unauthenticated file read, and no cross-tenant bypass of room membership on the main message routes. The one code-execution path (VULN-027, critical) needs an integration-management permission: integration scripts escape the isolated-vm sandbox because the isolate is handed the host `ivm` module and a host function Reference. It is kept over the admin-only filter because it crosses the boundary the vendor built for exactly that role, and because the integration permissions are designed to be delegated.

The most actionable findings in the shipped configuration are VULN-057 (any user raises any numeric setting through `statistics.telemetry`, widening the TOTP window and lifting lockouts; a one-line allow-list fixes it), VULN-001 (anonymous Livechat visitor registration returns an existing customer's token by phone number), VULN-073 and VULN-078 (an anonymous ReDoS in the mailer reached through the offline form, and a rate-limit bucket keyed on a header the caller writes, so one anonymous client blocks every web login while a rotating header escapes the limits altogether), and VULN-004 with VULN-033 (a stolen session reads the TOTP seed and survives the victim's password change). Behind off-by-default features, VULN-044 (CAS session fixation) and VULN-002 (OAuth email meld into the env-created administrator) are account takeovers.

Two patterns run through the list and are worth more than any single finding. The first is authorization decided on an object the caller named rather than the object being accessed: VULN-076 is the clearest case, where a Livechat visitor's own room authorises a subscription to someone else's. The second is a fix applied to one call site and not to its siblings: VULN-075 and VULN-081 are two unguarded outbound fetches beside two that the vendor guarded, VULN-077 is the endpoint a token-projection fix missed, and VULN-079 is an input-validation fix applied per method rather than at the model. A maintainer reading this report will get more out of the four sibling cases than out of four separate patches.

Verification depth: every cited file:line was re-read at the pinned commit, every excerpt in `findings/` is copied from the target by line range (a stale range fails the build, so the excerpts cannot drift from the source), and the CVSS band is checked against the vector for every finding. No finding was run in this stage; statuses are source-traced, so 46 confirmed vulnerabilities and 18 likely ones go to stage 11 for dynamic validation, 9 need something the sealed lab cannot provide (an Enterprise licence, an external network or a third-party provider; each carries a `manual_reason`), 10 were filtered or disproved and 1 is documented behaviour. Expansion corrected one finding's own claim: VULN-080's title said the sanitiser that fixed CVE-2022-21830 was gone, and reading the file showed DOMPurify still imported and applied on the emoji-insertion path but not on the write that re-parses the visitor's text, with `shouldComponentUpdate` making a paste into an empty composer the trigger rather than typing. Known versus novel among the real findings: 61 novel, 12 known and still unpatched in this build, each cited per finding.

findings.title: IDOR in anonymous Livechat visitor registration: a customer's phone number returns their visitor token, their email rebinds it
findings.category: Broken access control (credential disclosure by user-controlled key)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an unauthenticated caller turned a customer's phone number into their Livechat token and read their conversation, and an email address stole the record from the customer outright)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven unauthenticated on the shipped build for the disclosure and rebind legs, and with Omnichannel on for the read; the key is a customer's phone number.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-01: searched the vendor tracker and OSV (npm @rocket.chat/meteor and rocket.chat at 9.1.0-develop: 0 advisories). Adjacent only: issue #42478 (rebind by visitor id, closed without fix, does not cover the phone or email branch), GHSA-cqj7-h8cj-jmf2 / CVE-2026-49278 (token returned by visitors.info, fixed 8.5.0), CVE-2026-65644 (visitor name HTML, fixed 8.8.0).
findings.conditional_on: Omnichannel in use, so that real visitors with phone numbers or emails exist (the endpoint itself answers with Livechat_enabled off)
findings.impact: High (CVSS 8.2): unauthenticated, no victim interaction, full read of one customer's support history per request. Anyone who knows a customer's phone number receives that customer's visitor token, the only Livechat credential, and with it reads their conversations and transcripts and posts as them; a known email address instead re-keys the customer's visitor record to the attacker's token, so the attacker owns it and the customer's own token stops resolving.
findings.remediation: In registerGuest (packages/omni-core/src/visitor/create.ts:105-115) create a new visitor when the caller's token is unknown instead of merging into a visitor found by phone or email; move returning-customer linking to the agent-side contact merge; never return token to a caller that did not present it (project it out of the livechat/visitor response); refuse the route while Livechat_enabled is false. This is the object-level check deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (Mitigation) prescribes: resolve the visitor from the credential the caller presented, never from a key the caller supplies.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the feature and removes only the weakness: returning customers who lost their browser token are no longer re-attached to their old visitor record automatically (an agent merges the contact instead), and the route refuses registration while Omnichannel is off.

findings.title: OAuth account linking by unverified email claim, so an IdP identity melds into any local account with that address
findings.category: Authentication bypass (federated account linking on an unverified email claim)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an identity provider asserting an administrator's email address, with no verification claim, yielded a full administrator session and reset that administrator's own password)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven end to end in the lab: an unverified email claim from a configured provider gave a full administrator session and reset the owner's password.
findings.known_evidence: Vendor declined for now: in the review thread of PR #43840 (merged 2026-11-20, in this build) Rocket.Chat member yash-rajpal answered the finding that custom OAuth logins link existing accounts by email without provider verification: 'it is a known issue and being discussed internally by the team. For now it has been decided to leave it like this'. No CVE, GHSA or fix; affects 9.1.0-develop at 9f3d6c8c. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/pull/43840
findings.conditional_on: an OAuth login provider enabled (GitHub, Google, GitLab, Apple, or Custom OAuth with the oauth-enterprise module)
findings.impact: High (CVSS 7.4): account takeover without the victim's password, bounded by whether the IdP can be made to assert the address. An attacker who makes a configured provider assert a victim's email is linked to the victim's local account and, when no second factor applies to it (the env-created administrator is exactly such an account, inserted with no services), the OAuth callback issues a login code for the victim. Even when 2FA stops the login the IdP link persists and the victim's address is marked verified, and a password account whose address was unverified has its password forcibly reset.
findings.remediation: In accounts_meld.js:14-31 link only when the provider asserts the address as verified (OIDC email_verified, GitHub's verified primary email, GitLab confirmed_at, Apple email_verified) and otherwise refuse with a sign-in-and-link instruction; carry the verification flag through configureOAuthServices.ts:39-50 instead of dropping it; evaluate each provider's merge switch before any write and default it off, and give the built-in GitLab provider a keyField so the customOAuth.ts:263-300 hook that honours Accounts_OAuth_Gitlab_merge_users actually runs. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (federated identity: never trust an unverified claim to bind an account).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps social login and removes only the weakness: users whose IdP does not assert a verified address, and users who never linked, sign in once with their password and link from their profile; silent first-login merging stops for those providers, and a workspace that relied on it must link accounts explicitly.

findings.title: Cross-user event injection on notify-room-users: any member forges userData and video-conference events into every other member's private stream
findings.category: Broken access control on a realtime channel (cross-user event injection)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (one ordinary member injected a forced logout, a user-document rewrite (name and roles) and a forged incoming call into another member's private realtime channel)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #42669 (filed 2026-10-09) reports the unvalidated video-conference relay; its fix PR #42754 is open and not in this build (notifications.module.ts:299-317 relays both events unvalidated at 9f3d6c8c). Residual of GHSA-r3v3-v742-55j5 (fixed 8.8.0 and backports, whose allow-list is at notifications.module.ts:304-308). The userData leg is in no public report. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/42669
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.4): one DDP call from an ordinary account hits every online member of a shared room. A forged userData removed event makes their web clients discard stored credentials and drop to the login page (repeatable, so a persistent nuisance outage timed to push users at a phishing login); a forged updated event rewrites the client-side user record other members hold (displayed roles, status, profile); a forged video-conference call event rings them with an incoming call attributed to any user, including an administrator. Server-side sessions stay valid and nothing is read, so the loss is integrity and availability of other users' clients.
findings.remediation: In notifications.module.ts:300-317 drop userData from the relay (no shipped client writes it) and run relayed video-conference events through VideoConf.validateAction with uid equal to this.userId, exactly as the direct notify-user write at :319-343 already does; better, give streamUser an emit rule so notify-user/<uid>/userData carries only server-produced events. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/WebSocket_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (message-level authorization and input validation on every frame).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps call ringing between room members and removes only the weakness: relayed userData events stop being delivered (no first-party client sends them, and the real ones come from the server), and malformed or impersonated call events are refused instead of forwarded.

findings.title: users.info returns the caller's raw services document, disclosing the TOTP seed and backup-code hashes to any holder of the session
findings.category: Sensitive data exposure (second-factor secret disclosed to the session)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a session read its own account's TOTP seed and backup-code hashes from users.info, and a code derived from that seed passed the second factor)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-04: searched for users.info TOTP secret exposure; adjacent only HackerOne #842625 (users.info leaked the reset hash, fixed by PR #17238), CVE-2021-22911 and CVE-2022-32211 (2FA secret through injection, fixed). PR #35549 narrowed services on /me only (stage 08 R-26).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.8): a one-off credential theft becomes durable control of the account. The self view of users.info returns services.totp.secret (the base32 TOTP seed) and services.totp.hashedBackup, so whoever holds the victim's token once can generate valid second-factor codes forever: after the stolen session is revoked they still pass every twoFactorRequired step-up (minting a 2FA-bypassing personal access token, changing the account email, disabling 2FA, deleting the account) and, with the password, future logins. OAuth provider tokens stored under services.<provider> are disclosed the same way.
findings.remediation: Build the self view of services in getFullUserData.ts:152-177 from the allow-list getUserInfo.ts:120-131 already uses for /me (totp.enabled, email2fa.enabled, password.exists, linked provider names) instead of projecting services:1 and deleting four keys, and never return services.totp.secret, services.totp.hashedBackup, emailCode, provider access tokens or cloud tokens from any endpoint once enrolment is finished. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (the TOTP seed is shown once at enrolment and never served again) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the endpoint and removes only the weakness: an API client that read raw services from users.info for its own account now gets booleans (the web client already reads /me, which is already filtered), and nothing can retrieve a seed after enrolment, so a client that re-displayed the QR code from users.info must re-enrol the user instead.

findings.title: Anonymous callers can read the permission-to-role map through the permissions/get method
findings.category: Unauthenticated information disclosure
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an unauthenticated DDP caller read the whole permission table (993 entries) with the roles that hold each permission)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Public issue #39821 '[Todo] permissions/get method allows unauthenticated access' (2026-03-23) and fix PR #39822 (closed unmerged by its author on 2026-03-24); the method still answers anonymously at 9f3d6c8c and its source keeps the TODO 'should we return this for non logged users?' (permissions/index.ts:38). No CVE, GHSA or fix. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/39821
findings.impact: An anonymous caller learns which roles hold which permissions and the names of custom roles; no account, data or capability is exposed.
findings.remediation: Return an empty list from permissions/get when this.userId is unset, as subscriptions/get does.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the method for logged-in clients; anonymous-read clients lose a map they cannot use.
findings.detail: Filtered (informational): permissions/get (permissions/index.ts:31-41) answers anonymous DDP and method.callAnon with the whole permission-to-role map, including custom role names, but it names no account, discloses no data and grants no capability, so there is no boundary to cross; subscriptions/get returns an empty list to an anonymous caller, which is the shape this method should have. Kept as a hardening note; a human may re-open it where custom role names are themselves sensitive.

findings.title: stream-apps and stream-importers accept anonymous subscriptions, and the app setting-changed event carries the new value (secrets included)
findings.category: Unauthenticated information disclosure (realtime)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an unauthenticated websocket held subscriptions to the app and importer administration streams, which a logged-in-only stream refuses)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-06: searched stream-importers / stream-apps unauthenticated subscription; adjacent only PRs #34922 and #35194 (preview check on stream-room-messages).
findings.conditional_on: an Apps-Engine app with settings installed, and an administrator changing one of its settings while the attacker is subscribed
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.9): an unauthenticated DDP socket held open collects the plaintext value of every Apps-Engine setting an administrator saves while it is subscribed. Those settings are where installed apps keep credentials for external systems (third-party API keys, webhook secrets, bot tokens), and the engine documents PASSWORD-type settings as not encrypted, so the value on the wire is the secret itself. Administrators save them at install time and on every rotation. The stream-importers leg additionally hands an anonymous listener the progress and record counts of any running import.
findings.remediation: In notifications.module.ts:365-371 replace allowRead('all') with a permission check: logged (plus manage-apps for administrative events) for streamApps and run-import for streamImporters, and set allowEmit accordingly; in listeners.module.ts:528-531 and the AppServerNotifier emit only { appId, settingId } so no value travels on a stream at all, letting the admin UI re-read the setting over the authorized REST route. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/WebSocket_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (authorize every subscription and message) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps both streams for authorized clients and removes only the weakness: anonymous sockets can no longer subscribe, and a setting-changed event no longer carries the value, so the admin settings page must re-read the setting after the event (one extra authorized request) instead of taking it from the frame.

findings.title: users.listByStatus leaks every account's email, roles and last login to any ordinary user, and sorts on client-chosen fields before projecting
findings.category: Authenticated data exposure (PII across teams)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an ordinary account read every account's email address, role list and last-login time, administrators included, and ordered the listing by a field the response never returns)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-07: searched users.listByStatus email disclosure; adjacent only CVE-2022-32219 (users.list query injection, fixed 4.7.5), CVE-2021-22892 and CVE-2020-28208 (email enumeration, fixed). Stage 08 R-27 links the residual client-chosen sort to CVE-2022-32219.
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): the lowest-privileged account enumerates the whole workspace directory. One paged call returns every user's email address, role assignments (which names the administrators) and last-login time, across every team, while the sibling users.list strips exactly those fields for the same caller. The address list is the input for the email-keyed attacks elsewhere in this report (OAuth email meld, Direct Reply spoofing, reset-mailbox 2FA bypass) and the roles say whom to aim them at; lastLogin shows which accounts are dormant. The client-chosen sort runs in MongoDB before the projection, so ordering also answers questions about fields the response never prints.
findings.remediation: Gate users.listByStatus on view-user-administration (or view-full-other-user-info) at users.ts:789 instead of view-d-room, build the projection in findPaginatedUsersByStatus from the caller's rights the way the users.list path does through parseJsonQuery.ts:41-48 (emails, roles, lastLogin and services are already in defaultLimitedUserFieldsToExclude for unprivileged callers), and accept sort only from an allow-list of fields that are actually projected. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Enforce Least Privileges) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.md (allow-list, not deny-list).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the admin Users page working for administrators and removes only the weakness: ordinary users lose an endpoint the web client never calls on their behalf (the admin screen is the only caller), and a request sorting on a field outside the allow-list gets a 400 instead of a silent privileged sort.

findings.title: Room-message stream authorization is never re-evaluated, so a previewer keeps receiving a channel's messages after it is made private
findings.category: Broken access control (authorization not re-evaluated after revocation)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an open stream subscription kept delivering a room's messages after the room was made private and every new read by the same user was refused)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-08: searched stream subscription persisting after a channel turns private; adjacent only open PR #43528 (delivery-time check for private discussions only) and merged PRs #34922 and #35194 (subscribe-time preview check).
findings.impact: Low (CVSS 3.1): making a public channel private is the owner's way to shut non-members out, and it does not shut out anyone already subscribed. A previewer who held a stream-room-messages subscription when the change happened keeps receiving every new message in that room for as long as the socket lives, while a fresh subscription from the same account is refused; the same holds when the channel's team becomes private or an administrator revokes preview-c-room from the role. What leaks is live message content of one room, bounded by the socket's lifetime (a reconnect ends it).
findings.remediation: Re-evaluate existing room-messages, notify-room and room-data subscriptions when the inputs to canReadRoom change (room type, team type, ABAC attributes, role permissions) and remove those that no longer pass, extending the _afterPublish revocation hook in notifications.module.ts:86-112 beyond the subscriber's own subscription document; or give streamRoomMessage an allowEmit rule that re-checks canReadRoom per delivery with a short per-connection cache instead of leaving it at the default allowEmit('all'). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/WebSocket_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (message-level authorization).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps realtime delivery and removes only the weakness: previewers lose the live feed at the moment their access changes rather than at their next reconnect, and a per-delivery check costs one cached permission lookup per message and subscriber (the subscription-removal variant costs nothing per message).

findings.title: Room ban not enforced on the notification and file-download paths, because both match the banned subscription
findings.category: Broken access control (ban not enforced on the notification and file paths)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a banned member kept receiving the room's new messages through notifications and downloaded its file, while the room's history refused it)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-09: searched banned users still receiving notifications and files; adjacent only PR #43318 (XMPP rooms ignoring bans), HackerOne #2028450 (banned user deleting messages), CVE-2026-48616 (a different check in the same file function).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): a room ban, the moderators' tool for shutting one person out of a room, leaks on two side paths. The banned account keeps receiving new-message notifications for that room, and a notification payload carries the message text and sender, so the banned user follows the conversation in real time while the history and stream routes correctly refuse them; and with the shipped members-only download mode they keep downloading the room's files by id. The account stays active, so no further step is needed; what leaks is the text of new messages in that one room and its attachments.
findings.remediation: Add status: { $exists: false } to the notification recipient query in sendNotificationsOnMessage.ts:292-299 so a marked subscription cannot be a recipient, and replace the members-only download check at FileUpload.ts:542-544 with the status-aware Subscriptions.countByRoomIdAndUserId (or with canAccessRoomIdAsync, which the sibling mode already uses); then audit the other call sites of the status-blind findOneByRoomIdAndUserId and give the model a status-aware variant so the next caller cannot repeat the mistake. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default, and Enforce Authorization Checks on Static Resources for the file route).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps notifications and file downloads for members and removes only the weakness: banned users stop receiving that room's notifications and can no longer fetch its files, which is what the ban already promises; no change for anyone who is not banned.

findings.title: Missing authorization on chat.getDeletedMessages: any user lists the deleted-message ids and timing of any room
findings.category: Missing authorization (room metadata disclosure)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (any authenticated account reads the deleted-message ids, count and timing of a private group it is refused every other way)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #42481 'chat.getDeletedMessages leaks deleted-message IDs of rooms the caller cannot access' (2026-10-01; closed 2026-10-02 by the vendor, 'we will track it'), same endpoint, root cause and reproduction; no fix merged, chat.ts:1016-1059 still has only authRequired at 9f3d6c8c. No CVE or GHSA. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/42481
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): any account that knows a room id, including a private group or a direct message it has no part in, learns how many messages were deleted there, when, and their ids, by paging since backwards. The content is not returned, so this is metadata: the activity pattern of a room the caller cannot open (who is cleaning up and when) plus message ids that feed the per-message routes elsewhere in this report. Room ids are not secrets; they appear in permalinks, invite payloads, notification payloads and the responses of several other routes.
findings.remediation: At the top of the handler (chat.ts:1036) refuse unless canAccessRoomIdAsync(roomId, this.userId) holds, the check the neighbouring history method performs before it reads anything (getChannelHistory.ts:39-42). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (look objects up within what the caller may reach).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the sync feature for members and removes only the weakness: a non-member gets 403 where it previously got a list, so a client that polled this route for rooms the user has since left stops receiving data for them.

findings.title: Typing indicators accept a room the caller cannot access, because the user-activity write rule only checks the claimed name
findings.category: Missing authorization on a realtime write
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an account refused both the history and the stream of a private group wrote activity events into it that the room's members received)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-11: searched typing indicator writes into inaccessible rooms; adjacent only GHSA-27jx-236m-3f5j and GHSA-r3v3-v742-55j5 (other stream writes), PR #41910 (federated typing).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): any account can write presence events into any room by id, including private groups and direct messages it cannot open. Members of that room see a non-member "is typing", which is a falsified presence state and a usable social-engineering prop (a name appearing in a confidential room suggests they are in it); the accepted write also raises the server-side room.user-activity event, which the premium federation layer forwards to remote servers, and acceptance versus refusal is an existence oracle for room ids. No message content is read or written.
findings.remediation: In canType (notifications.module.ts:228-271), or in the write rule that calls it at :273-285, require that the caller may access the room: load the room and refuse unless Authorization.canAccessRoom(room, user) passes, caching the answer per connection and room so a typing indicator still costs nothing per keystroke. The read side of the same stream already does exactly this at :199-226. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/WebSocket_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (authorize each message, not just the connection).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps typing indicators for room members and for Livechat visitors (the token branch is unchanged) and removes only the weakness: a write naming a room the caller cannot access is dropped, so a client that optimistically announced typing before its subscription landed may lose that first event.

findings.title: Mass assignment in rooms.mediaConfirm: a member sets any message type t, forging system notices that chat.sendMessage refuses
findings.category: Mass assignment (forged system notices)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an ordinary member stored two messages with attacker-chosen system types and text, which the ordinary send path refuses outright)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-12: sibling path of CVE-2026-106075 (chat.sendMessage mass assignment, fixed 9.0.0) and of GHSA-fhc2-x8cp-c5ch / CVE-2026-45687 (sendFileMessage allow-list, which still includes t); this file-message path is not reported.
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): an ordinary member posts messages that render as the server's own system notices in any room they can upload to. Confirming an upload with {"t":"r","msg":"Payroll-update-see-pinned-link"} renders as "Room name changed to Payroll-update-see-pinned-link" in system styling, and t:"ul" renders "User left this channel"; readers have no way to tell these from genuine server events, which makes them a strong in-workspace phishing and confusion primitive. The same field also admits t:"e2e", which satisfies the encrypted-room gate in sendMessage and so slips a plaintext message past the "no unencrypted messages in an encrypted room" rule.
findings.remediation: In sendFileMessage.ts:164-182 stop accepting an arbitrary t: restrict it to the literal e2e and accept it only when content is present and the room is encrypted, or call the same MessageTypes.isSystemMessage refusal the plain send route applies at chat.ts:965-967. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Mass_Assignment_Cheat_Sheet.md (allow-list the bindable fields; never bind a field that changes how the object is interpreted).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps file messages, captioned uploads and encrypted file messages and removes only the weakness: a client that sends any other t with a file receives error-invalid-arguments, and nothing can create a system-typed message through the upload path.

findings.title: Email Direct Reply takes the posting identity from the From header, so one spoofed email posts as any user under any message id
findings.category: Authentication bypass by spoofing (message impersonation)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the mail sink is in the lab but the poller interval could not be waited out inside this stage's time budget)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-13: searched direct reply email spoofed From; adjacent only PR #43777 (tests of processDirectEmail), CVE-2024-46936 (impersonation via UpdateOTRAck, a different path).
findings.conditional_on: Direct_Reply_Enable with an IMAP or POP reply mailbox configured
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.9): an outsider with no account posts a message as any Rocket.Chat user, administrators included, into any room that user can post to, threaded under a real message of the attacker's choosing. The posting identity comes from the email's From header and the thread from the +<messageId> tag in the recipient address, neither of which is a secret: the identity is an address (the directory listing elsewhere in this report hands out every one) and the message id travels in permalinks and notification mails. The result is high-trust impersonation inside the conversation being discussed ("Approved, go ahead" from the finance lead, in the thread), with sentByEmail set but no visible warning.
findings.remediation: Make the reply address itself the credential: generate replies+<mid>.<uid>.<exp>.<hmac>@domain when the notification is sent, verify the HMAC and expiry in processDirectEmail.ts before anything else, and post as the user named in the token while ignoring the From header entirely; optionally also require DKIM alignment for the sending domain. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (an identity claim is only an authenticator when the server can verify its issuer) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Email_Validation_and_Verification_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps Email Direct Reply and removes only the weakness: a reply sent from a different address than the one the notification went to, or to a notification older than the token's expiry, is no longer accepted, and users who forward a notification to a colleague to answer on their behalf lose that (undocumented) ability.

findings.title: External control of a file path in downloadPublicImportFile: any local path is read into the importer, and the error is an existence oracle
findings.category: External control of a file path (privileged importer)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a run-import holder read an arbitrary server-side file into the import store and distinguished existing from missing paths from the error alone, and the permission is delegable to an ordinary account)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #42355 'Arbitrary Local File Read via downloadPublicImportFile API' (2026-09-25, closed 2026-10-21 without a fix); fix PR #42357 'reject local paths in public import download' is open; this build keeps copyLocalFile and fs.existsSync (downloadPublicImportFile.ts:30-48). The sibling SSRF GHSA-6x96-99rg-wg67 on the same endpoint is fixed here. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/42355
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.9): a holder of run-import, which is an operator permission the product is designed to delegate rather than an administrator-only one, turns the importer into a filesystem reader. Any value that does not start with http is treated as a server path: a missing path comes back inside the error message (an existence oracle for the container's filesystem), and an existing one is copied into the import store and parsed, so its content surfaces in the import preview, the import's progress records and its error output. A directory path is handed to the importer as-is. Readable targets include the bundle's own configuration, mounted secrets and anything else the Node process can open.
findings.remediation: Resolve fileUrl with path.resolve against a configured import directory and refuse anything whose resolved path is not inside it, in executeDownloadPublicImportFile (downloadPublicImportFile.ts:35-47); apply the same containment to the stored name joined in getImportFileData.ts:58-61; and return one generic error for both missing and forbidden paths so the message stops echoing the probe. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Path_Traversal_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (canonicalise, then verify the prefix) with deploy/knowledge/payloads/PayloadsAllTheThings/Directory Traversal/README.md for the probe shapes.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps server-path imports and removes only the weakness: an operator must place the export file in the configured import directory (or use an HTTP URL, which already goes through the SSRF-checked fetch), and the error no longer names the path that was tried.

findings.title: MFA bypass through the recovery flow: resetPassword and verifyEmail are exempted from the second factor and return a session
findings.category: Authentication (MFA bypass through the recovery flow)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (the mailbox alone produced a working session on a TOTP-protected account; password login for the same account still demanded the code)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: the mailbox alone gave a working session on a TOTP-protected account, while the password path still demanded the code.
findings.known_evidence: HackerOne #1701378 'Bypassing 2FA with conventional session management' (disclosed, about 2022) reports the verifyEmail leg; issue #10183 (2018, closed 2023-04-18 without a fix) names the reset bypass. This build still exempts both at 2fa/loginHandler.ts:23-24. No advisory, no fix. https://hackerone.com/reports/1701378
findings.impact: High (CVSS 7.4): for an account protected with TOTP, the mailbox alone is enough to take it over. The onValidateLogin callback that enforces the second factor returns early for the password login produced by resetPassword and for verifyEmail, and Meteor's handlers for both hand back a login token, so an emailed reset link yields a full session without any code. That defeats the exact threat 2FA was enrolled against (someone who has the password or the mailbox), and the same session can then read the account's TOTP seed through another finding in this report, making the compromise permanent.
findings.remediation: Let resetPassword and verifyEmail perform their action without issuing a session when the account has an active second factor (wrap Meteor's handlers, or move the reset to a REST route that does), or require a TOTP or backup code in the reset form itself; then remove the two exemptions at 2fa/loginHandler.ts:22-23 so the callback covers the recovery path like every other login. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (a recovery flow must not be a way around the second factor) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps password reset and email verification and removes only the weakness: a user with 2FA enrolled signs in once more after resetting, presenting their second factor, and a user who has lost that factor uses the administrator reset path that already exists; users without 2FA see no change at all.

findings.title: mailer.unsubscribe accepts any user id together with that user's creation time in milliseconds as the only secret
findings.category: Predictable capability token
findings.status: FAILED (the capability exists but is not reachable: the response is identical for a right and a wrong value, the only secret is a millisecond out of 86,400,000, and the route allowed 40 blind attempts before refusing)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The capability exists but the response is identical for a right and a wrong value, so there is nothing to aim at.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-16: searched mailer.unsubscribe createdAt; no report of the endpoint.
findings.impact: A user could opt another user out of administrator Mailer announcements if they guess that user's creation time to the millisecond.
findings.remediation: Unsubscribe this.userId when logged in, and use a random or HMAC token per user for the emailed link.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the feature; old unsubscribe links stop working once the token format changes.
findings.detail: Filtered (brute force): mailer.unsubscribe (mailer.ts:54-72, Users.ts:2250-2262) accepts any user id with that user's createdAt in milliseconds as the only secret, but the guess is blind (the route answers the same either way), capped at one call per minute, and worth only opting a victim out of administrator announcements. Re-open it if createdAt turns out to be exposed by another endpoint, which would make the secret known rather than guessed.

findings.title: REST takes the client address from a client-supplied X-Real-IP when X-Forwarded-For is absent or HTTP_FORWARDED_COUNT is 0, so per-IP rate limits and the failed-login IP block follow the header
findings.category: Use of a less trusted source (client address spoofing)
findings.status: INTENDED (behind the reverse proxy the vendor's guide prescribes, the client address comes from the proxy's X-Forwarded-For and a spoofed X-Real-IP does not move the limiter; the vendor documents stripping that header as the proxy's job)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Measured in the documented deployment: behind the prescribed proxy the header had no effect, and the vendor documents stripping it as the proxy's job.
findings.known_evidence: Vendor position in https://docs.rocket.chat/docs/security-guidelines: 'Rocket.Chat prioritizes the X-Real-Ip header when determining the clientAddress', 'Misconfigured proxies could allow users to bypass rate limiting and other security measures', 'Ensure that your proxies and load balancers ignore the X-Real-Ip header when making requests from end users'. No advisory or fix; documented behaviour (stage 07 F-17).
findings.impact: On deployments whose proxy passes a client X-Real-IP through (or with no proxy), per-IP limits and the failed-login IP block key on a value the client chooses.
findings.remediation: Never read X-Real-IP in getRemoteAddress; use the socket address when the count is 0 and the HTTP_FORWARDED_COUNT-th X-Forwarded-For entry otherwise, as the DDP server does.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the feature; a proxy that sets only X-Real-IP must also append X-Forwarded-For.
findings.detail: Intended (documented): the vendor's security guidelines state that Rocket.Chat prioritises X-Real-Ip when determining clientAddress and that proxies must ignore that header from end users, so a deployment where it reaches remoteAddressMiddleware.ts:17-40 from a client is a proxy misconfiguration, not a product flaw. One residual for a human: the direct, proxy-less deployment that docs/features/oauth2-server.md:57 recommends has nobody to strip the header.

findings.title: /oauth/userinfo accepts expired access tokens for 30 days, because only the REST bearer path checks expires
findings.category: Session management (credential used after expiry)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an access token past its expiry still returned the account's identity from /oauth/userinfo, while the REST bearer path refused the same token)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-18: searched /oauth/userinfo expired token; adjacent only GHSA-39hg-492f-3c4f / CVE-2026-49277 (tokens surviving deactivation, fixed 8.5.0 by PR #40524, which added findOneActiveById to userinfo but no expiry check).
findings.conditional_on: an administrator-created OAuth app with a relying party that signs users in from /oauth/userinfo
findings.impact: Low (CVSS 3.7): a Rocket.Chat-issued OAuth access token keeps identifying its user at /oauth/userinfo after it has expired, until a TTL index removes the record 30 days later. The endpoint returns sub, name, email, email_verified, preferred username and avatar URL, so a leaked expired token (from a log, a browser history, a proxy cache, a mobile app's storage) still yields that user's identity; and a relying party that signs users in from userinfo alone, which is a common pattern, accepts a credential Rocket.Chat itself would refuse on its REST API. The same token is correctly rejected by /api/v1/*, which is what makes this an inconsistency rather than a design choice.
findings.remediation: Factor the expiry test out of oAuth2ServerAuth (oauth2-server.ts:41-43) into a shared helper and call it in the /oauth/userinfo handler before resolving the user, so both paths read the same rule; the TTL index on expires should also not be read as a validity window (OAuthAccessTokens.ts:17 keeps records 30 days past expiry for audit, not for use). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/OAuth2_Cheat_Sheet.md (validate the token, including its lifetime, at every resource server endpoint) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: No change for valid tokens and no feature is removed: a client presenting an expired token gets 401 from userinfo exactly as it already does from the REST API, and must refresh, which every OAuth client already implements.

findings.title: Improper authentication on /hooks: any integration id and token authenticate, and the add and remove sub-routes skip the enabled and impersonation checks
findings.category: Authentication (credential accepted outside its purpose)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a webhook credential the administrator had revoked was refused by the posting route but still authenticated on /hooks/add, where it created an enabled outgoing integration that forwarded the channel to our listener)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: a revoked webhook credential still created an enabled outgoing integration that exfiltrated the channel.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-19: searched incoming webhook outgoing token add remove disabled; adjacent only issue #4773 (logging disabled incoming webhooks).
findings.conditional_on: integrations exist, and the integration's post-as user holds manage-outgoing-integrations or manage-own-outgoing-integrations
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.5): a webhook credential is accepted outside the purpose it was issued for. The lookup behind every /hooks route matches an integration by id and token with no type or enabled condition, so a disabled incoming webhook's URL still authenticates (the administrator's revocation only stops the posting route) and an outgoing integration's token, which the server sends to its own receiver in every payload, authenticates too. The add and remove sub-routes then run with the integration's user and skip the enabled and message-impersonate checks the posting route applies, so the holder of such a URL creates an outgoing integration pointed at their own listener and receives the watched rooms' messages continuously, or deletes existing integrations.
findings.remediation: Filter the credential lookup to the purpose: in the /hooks authenticatedRoute (webhooks.ts:400-416) require { type: 'webhook-incoming', enabled: true }, and apply the posting route's guards (the enabled test and the message-impersonate check at webhooks.ts:227-238) inside the add, remove and info handlers as well, so no sub-route is weaker than the primary one. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Webhook_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (scope a webhook secret to one direction and one purpose) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps incoming and outgoing webhooks working and removes only the weakness: a disabled webhook stops authenticating on every sub-route (which is what disabling already implies), an outgoing integration's token stops being accepted on /hooks (no first-party client sends it there), and add and remove now require the integration user's permissions.

findings.title: Authorization oracle in roles.addUserToRole: the already-in-role answer precedes the permission check, revealing any user's roles in any room
findings.category: Information disclosure (authorization oracle)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an unprivileged account read out global and room-scoped role membership, including the owner of a private group it cannot see, from the error code alone)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-20: searched roles.addUserToRole already-in-role disclosure; adjacent only PR #22407 (added the check), PR #42947 (team role checks).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): any account can ask, one question at a time, whether a named user holds a named role, globally or scoped to a room id, and read the answer from which error comes back. error-user-already-in-role means yes, error-action-not-allowed means no. That enumerates the global administrators and, with room ids, the owners and moderators of rooms the caller cannot see, which is the targeting information the role-demotion, account-takeover and phishing findings in this report need. Nothing is written: a caller without access-permissions never reaches the mutation.
findings.remediation: Declare permissionsRequired: ['access-permissions'] on the roles.addUserToRole route (roles.ts:113-128) so the framework refuses before the handler runs, instead of relying on the check inside addUserToRole (addUserToRole.ts:10-15) which is reached only after hasRoleAsync has answered. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default, and Verify that Authorization Checks are Performed in the Right Location: before any side effect or observable branch).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps role assignment working for callers who hold access-permissions and removes only the weakness: an unauthorized caller receives 403 immediately instead of an error that distinguishes the two cases, so a client that relied on error-user-already-in-role to pre-check membership must use the roles listing instead.

findings.title: Uploads render inline on the workspace origin under a CSP without sandbox or form-action, and the type deny list matches only the declared string
findings.category: Protection mechanism failure (same-origin user content)
findings.status: FAILED (content-type 'text/html', collector hit=False)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Disproved on this build: the upload is served with Content-Disposition attachment and a default-src 'none' policy, so nothing renders.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-21: searched upload served inline, SVG deny list bypass; adjacent only HackerOne #368927 (2018 SVG upload phishing), HackerOne #1380157 (CSP bypass with an uploaded script), the SSD desktop-client advisory. PR #38106 validates renamed files in the browser only (stage 08 R-28).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.4): a member uploads an HTML page and shares a link with ?contentDisposition=inline, and the victim's browser renders attacker-authored markup on the workspace's own origin, logged in, with the address bar showing the real workspace. The response's CSP is default-src 'none' alone, and form-action does not fall back to default-src, so a credential form inside that page submits to the attacker; scripts are blocked while that CSP holds, so this is same-origin phishing rather than stored XSS today, and any future loosening of the file CSP turns it into XSS beside the staff's session tokens. The shipped deny list is the single string image/svg+xml compared exactly, so an SVG body declared application/xml is accepted and served as XML, which browsers render as SVG.
findings.remediation: Send a complete CSP for user content in requests.ts:53 (default-src 'none'; sandbox; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'), force attachment for HTML, XML and SVG regardless of the contentDisposition query (helper.ts:15-21), and validate the type by file signature rather than by the declared string (restrictions.ts:21-38 with mimeTypes.ts:20-29); serving user content from a separate origin is the structural fix. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.md (file-signature validation, serving from a different domain, forcing download) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Content_Security_Policy_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps uploads and the inline preview of images, PDF, audio and video, and removes only the weakness: HTML, XML and SVG attachments download instead of rendering, and an upload whose bytes do not match its declared type is rejected, so a client that relied on sending a wrong Content-Type must send the right one.

findings.title: Unintended proxy in /avatar: the decoded request path is interpolated into the provider URL and every upstream header is relayed on the workspace origin
findings.category: Unintended proxy (header and path pass-through)
findings.status: FAILED (the traversal answered HTTP 200 with content-type 'image/svg+xml' and our marker absent)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The traversal reached the provider but the workspace re-encoded the response as an image, so no attacker HTML was served from its origin.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-22: searched external avatar provider proxy headers; adjacent only issues #32812 and #18657.
findings.conditional_on: Accounts_AvatarExternalProviderUrl set (an external avatar provider configured)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.7): with an external avatar provider configured, /avatar/<anything> becomes an open relay for that provider's host. The username is the decoded request path, so %2F, %3F and %23 reach the URL template as /, ? and #, which lets a crafted link address another path on the provider; and the handler copies every upstream response header onto the workspace's own response, Content-Type and Set-Cookie included, with no CSP of its own. Where the provider host serves any attacker-influenced content (profile pages, user uploads, a CDN bucket), that content is delivered as same-origin HTML from the workspace, which is script execution next to every logged-in user's session, and provider cookies land on the workspace domain.
findings.remediation: encodeURIComponent the username before substituting it into the template and refuse names containing a slash (user.ts:12-19, user.ts:28-29); copy only an allow-list of response headers (Content-Type restricted to image/*, Content-Length, ETag, Last-Modified and the caching headers) and add Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none' to the relayed response. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (never build an outbound URL from unencoded user input; constrain what comes back) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps external avatar providers and removes only the weakness: a provider that returns something other than an image, or that relies on cookies passing through, stops working through the proxy, and avatar paths containing encoded slashes are rejected rather than traversed.

findings.title: /livechat is served with no CSP even while Omnichannel is disabled, and its embed allowlist is enforced only when a Referer arrives
findings.category: Protection mechanism failure (hardening)
findings.status: FAILED (the CSP is genuinely absent from /livechat, but nothing exploitable follows on a default install: X-Frame-Options still blocks cross-origin framing and no parameter of the page is reflected, so there is no injection for the missing policy t)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The CSP is genuinely absent from /livechat, but nothing exploitable follows on a default install.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-23: searched /livechat CSP removed and the Referer-based framing control; adjacent only PR #17419, issue #20251, PR #29278, issue #19815.
findings.impact: Any future HTML injection in the widget would run without a CSP; the allowlist bypass needs Iframe_Restrict_Access turned off.
findings.remediation: Always send frame-ancestors built from the allowlist, give the page a nonce-based script policy, and return 404 while Livechat_enabled is false.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the widget; unlisted sites cannot embed it even when they strip the Referer.
findings.detail: Filtered (hardening without an exploitable path): livechat.ts:46-75 omits the CSP on a Referer-less request to /livechat and serves the page even while Omnichannel is off, but X-Frame-Options sameorigin still blocks cross-origin framing in the shipped configuration, and the missing CSP needs an injection to matter. Kept as the mitigating control the widget self-XSS finding is missing; the embed-allowlist leg needs Iframe_Restrict_Access turned off, which is a security control and so not a finding.

findings.title: Protected file downloads and personal data exports are marked publicly cacheable for a year, so a shared cache serves them to other people
findings.category: Sensitive data in a shared cache
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a private room's upload, which the workspace refuses to an unauthenticated caller, was served from a standard shared cache to a caller with no credentials, because the response says public, max-age=31536000)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven through a standard shared cache: the product's own headers are enough to serve a private upload to a stranger.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-24: searched file-upload Cache-Control max-age private files cached; adjacent only PR #43168 (tests that pin the header on /data-export).
findings.conditional_on: a shared HTTP cache (CDN or caching reverse proxy) in front of the whole workspace that honours Cache-Control
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.9): both responses are authorized per request (by cookie, query parameter or auth headers) and then sent with Cache-Control: max-age=31536000 and no private directive and no Vary: Cookie. A standards-following shared cache in front of the workspace, which the vendor's own deployment guide anticipates (a CDN or caching reverse proxy), may therefore store a private room's file or a complete personal data export and serve it to the next requester for the same URL, with no credential at all. The export case is the worse one: it is one archive containing a user's whole message history and their uploaded files.
findings.remediation: Mark the responses correctly: Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000 for protected uploads (requests.ts:53-54) and Cache-Control: no-store for personal data exports (userDataDownload.ts:50-51), and add Vary: Cookie where a cache might still key on the URL alone. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Web_Cache_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (an access-controlled response is never shared-cacheable) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.md (Cache-Control).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps both features and removes only the weakness: shared caches and CDNs stop storing protected files, so those requests reach the origin (more origin traffic and bandwidth for image-heavy workspaces), while browsers still cache them privately; data exports are no longer cached anywhere, so a user re-downloading one fetches it again.

findings.title: Integration script functions run with no timeout on the server's main thread
findings.category: Resource exhaustion (admin-authored code)
findings.status: FAILED (the script ran for 7.46s with no server-side bound (bystander latency up to 6.63s), but its author is the integration manager who wrote it: filtered as administrator-authored code, as the report has it)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Reproduces: a script ran for seven seconds with no server-side bound. Filed as informational because its author is the integration manager who wrote it.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #18542 'Endless loop in WebHook Script freezes Rocket.Chat instance' (open since 2020-08-12, no fix); in the isolated-vm engine the same effect comes from applySync with no timeout (isolated-vm.ts:17-25). https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/18542
findings.impact: A looping script written by an administrator freezes the server on the next webhook call.
findings.remediation: Pass a timeout to applySync (for example 3000 ms, as at compile time) or use apply with a timeout.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps scripts; scripts that legitimately run longer than the limit fail.
findings.detail: Filtered (administrator-authored code): applySync with no timeout (isolated-vm.ts:17-25) freezes the server on the next webhook call, but only for a script an integration manager wrote, so the actor and the author are the same person; publicly known as issue #18542, open since 2020. The boundary-crossing finding for that same role, the integration sandbox escape, is filed separately.

findings.title: Workspace-wide denial of service from one message: the markdown parser is super-quadratic and the attachment-description parse has no length cap
findings.category: Denial of service (inefficient algorithmic complexity)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (one ordinary member's message held the server for 3.05s at 4000 characters and 6.97s as an attachment description past the message-size limit, while a bystander's request waited up to 2.78s)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: one member's message cost seven seconds of server time and a bystander's request waited nearly three.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-26: parent CVE-2024-46935 / GHSA-6375-pg5j-8wph (message-parser < 0.31.30, fix PR #33227); OSV for @rocket.chat/message-parser@0.33.0 returns 0, so the parent fix is in; the residual cost and the uncapped description parse are not reported.
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.5): Rocket.Chat's server is single-threaded, and the markdown parse runs synchronously on the request that saves a message, so the parse time is an outage for every user. Stage 03 measured the bundled parser at about 9.8 s for 5000 asterisks and about 103 s for 20000: during that time no REST call, DDP frame or stream delivery is served, workspace-wide. The message body has a parse-length gate, but the first attachment's description is parsed with no length check at all, and chat.sendMessage places no maxLength on attachment items, so the cheapest path is an attachment description rather than a message body. The attack is repeatable at the shipped send limit.
findings.remediation: Apply getMessageMaxParseLength() to every field the hook parses, not just message.msg (BeforeSaveMarkdownParser.ts:31-44); cap attachment descriptions at Message_MaxAllowedSize in validateMessage (sendMessage.ts:131-164, where attachments are already validated) and give the REST attachment items a maxLength; and bound the parser's own work, either by making the tokenizer linear or by running it with a time budget off the event loop and falling back to plain text. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Denial_of_Service_Cheat_Sheet.md (input validation and bounded work per request; do not let one request monopolise a shared thread).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps markdown rendering and removes only the weakness: an attachment description longer than the cap is refused (or stored as plain text rather than parsed), and a pathological input renders unformatted instead of blocking the server; no legitimate message changes.

findings.title: isolated-vm sandbox escape in integration scripts: the isolate is handed the ivm module and a host-function Reference, giving code execution as the server
findings.category: Sandbox escape (remote code execution by integration managers)
findings.status: FAILED (the handles are exposed as the source says, but isolated-vm 6.2.0 refuses every navigation step (get on a function reference, deref, cross-isolate deref, result references), so no host-realm execution is reachable)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The handles are exposed exactly as the source says, but isolated-vm 6.2.0 refused every navigation step, so no host-realm execution was reachable in this build.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-27: searched integration script sandbox escape isolated-vm ivm Reference RCE; OSV isolated-vm@6.2.0: 0. Adjacent only GHSA-864f-rcv7-6rh4 (an isolated-vm C++ escape needing a shared Reference) and the vm2-era integration-script RCE chain (CVE-2021-22911).
findings.impact: Critical (CVSS 9.1): the isolated-vm engine exists to keep administrator-written integration scripts out of the server process, and this hands them the keys. buildSandbox puts the host ivm module itself into the isolate's global and exposes serverFetch as an ivm.Reference wrapping a host-realm async function; isolated-vm documents that a Reference's get and apply return further References for non-transferable values, so a script walks serverFetch.getSync('constructor') (the host AsyncFunction) to its constructor (the host Function) and calls it to execute arbitrary code in the main isolate, where process is in scope. That is the database credentials, every room's content, the environment and the container, reached from a permission the product is designed to delegate.
findings.remediation: Stop placing host-realm objects in the isolate: drop jail.setSync('ivm', ivm) (and the data === ivm exemption in isTransferable at buildSandbox.ts:74-79), and expose serverFetch as an ivm.Callback, or as a Reference the host side invokes with { arguments: { copy: true }, result: { copy: true, promise: true } }, so only copies cross the boundary; pass an explicit timeout to every apply. Grounding: isolated-vm's own security note against passing References to untrusted code, plus deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Nodejs_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (do not rely on an in-process sandbox that shares objects with the host).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps integration scripts and serverFetch and removes only the weakness: a script that used the ivm global or Reference methods directly stops working (no shipped example does, and the compatibility wrapper does not expose them), and serverFetch arguments and results are copies rather than live host objects, so a script can no longer mutate a host object it received.

findings.title: Indirect prompt injection in AI Search: other users' messages become instructions, and the answer renders as markdown that fetches attacker URLs
findings.category: LLM prompt injection (indirect, through retrieved content) with a rendering sink
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (AI Search needs a licensed AI module and a model provider, neither of which exists in this workspace)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-28: searched AI search prompt injection answer markdown image exfiltration; adjacent only CVE-2026-47733 (ImageElement javascript: URLs, fixed 8.5.0).
findings.conditional_on: the AI licence module with AI Search enabled and an OpenAI-compatible provider configured
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.4): the AI Search answer is built by concatenating the bodies of other users' messages into one user turn behind a plain "Source messages (untrusted):" label, with nothing escaping the per-source block structure, so a planted message can close its own block and address the model directly. The answer is then rendered through MarkdownText with DOMPurify allowing http(s) URIs, and the workspace CSP sets img-src * data: blob:, so a markdown image in the answer is fetched by the victim's browser on render. An attacker therefore steers what a colleague's AI answer says (fabricated statements with citations, phishing links) and can exfiltrate the text of the other retrieved sources, which may come from rooms the attacker cannot read, through the image URL.
findings.remediation: Neutralise retrieved content before it enters the prompt in buildSearchAnswerPrompt (llm.ts:51-67): fence each source in delimiters that are escaped inside the text, and strip markdown image and link syntax from the source bodies; and validate the output, rendering the answer in SearchAnswerPanel with a renderer that drops images and external links (or allows only the cited message permalinks). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (treat retrieved content as data, constrain the output surface) with deploy/knowledge/payloads/PayloadsAllTheThings/Prompt Injection/README.md for the injection shapes.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps AI answers and their citations and removes only the weakness: images and arbitrary external links no longer render inside an answer (citations still link to the cited messages), and source text reaches the model without markdown formatting, which does not change its meaning.

findings.title: SAML assertion decryption re-enables the insecure algorithms xml-encryption 4 disables
findings.category: Use of a risky cryptographic algorithm (library hardening switched off)
findings.status: FAILED (the SAML module is not present on this unlicensed workspace and every malformed assertion answers identically (1 distinct answer(s)), so the re-enabled algorithms expose no oracle: hardening, as the report has it)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Every malformed assertion answers identically and the module is absent, so the weakened algorithm list has no oracle: hardening, not a flaw.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-29: searched SAML xml-encryption disallowDecryptionWithInsecureAlgorithm; OSV xml-encryption@4.0.1: 0; the choice is recorded only in the vendor's code comment.
findings.impact: The SP decrypts AES-CBC, 3DES and RSA-1_5 payloads that the library refuses by default; exploitation would need an oracle the SP does not expose.
findings.remediation: Leave disallowDecryptionWithInsecureAlgorithm at its default and make legacy algorithms an explicit per-provider opt-in.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps SAML; IdPs that only emit CBC or 3DES assertions need an administrator opt-in.
findings.detail: Filtered (theoretical, no oracle): Response.ts:245-247 sets disallowDecryptionWithInsecureAlgorithm false, so the SP decrypts the AES-CBC, 3DES and RSA-1_5 payloads xml-encryption 4 refuses by default, but every SAML validation failure ends in the same redirect to / (SAML.ts:515-520, 576-579), so no padding or decryption oracle is exposed and the feature needs the enterprise saml licence. A hardening fix; re-open it if an error-distinguishing path is found.

findings.title: Deactivated and pending-approval accounts get working tokens through the OAuth login-code path, which bypasses validateLoginAttempt, and REST never re-checks active
findings.category: Authentication bypass through an alternate path (account state not enforced)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an account the administrator had deactivated signed in through the OAuth login-code path and its token read and wrote as that account, while the password path refused it)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: a deactivated account signed in through the OAuth path and posted, while the password path refused it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-30: searched deactivated user OAuth login token; adjacent (other paths, all fixed): GHSA-39hg-492f-3c4f / CVE-2026-49277, GHSA-6g3w-vg5p-w892 / CVE-2026-45757 (whose advisory notes REST checks no active), GHSA-7qr6-q62g-hm63 / CVE-2026-30831.
findings.conditional_on: an OAuth login provider enabled (GitHub, Google, GitLab, Apple web, or Custom OAuth with the EE module)
findings.impact: High (CVSS 7.1): the two account-state controls administrators rely on, deactivation for offboarding and manual approval for gatekeeping, do not hold for anyone who can sign in through a configured provider. Meteor's validateLoginAttempt refuses an inactive account, but the Passport callback never enters that pipeline: it mints a login code (or a 2FA challenge) for whatever user the upsert returned, loginCode.redeem turns the code into a login token through issueLoginToken, which only writes the hash, and REST authentication then finds the user by token and id with no active condition. A deactivated user therefore reads and posts in every room they belonged to and can mint personal access tokens; with manual approval on, an unapproved account gets a working session.
findings.remediation: Put the state rules where tokens are made and used: have issueLoginToken load the user and refuse active !== true and type === 'app' (and run the failed-login and onValidateLogin callbacks there, or route the Passport result through a Meteor login handler so the existing pipeline applies), and add active: true to the token lookup in ApiClass.authenticatedRoute (ApiClass.ts:894-902), which the OAuth-bearer branch already does with findOneActiveById. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default; Validate the Permissions on Every Request) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps social login and removes only the weakness: a deactivated or unapproved account can no longer obtain or use a token on any path, and every authenticated REST request matches one extra indexed field, which is negligible; a workspace that deliberately let deactivated users keep API access (no documented use) loses it.

findings.title: SAML assertions are not bound to this service provider: no Audience, Recipient, Destination or InResponseTo check, so another SP's assertion logs in
findings.category: Authentication bypass (assertion not bound to its intended recipient)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (SAML is a licensed enterprise module and is not present on this unlicensed workspace)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-31: searched SAML Audience Recipient Destination InResponseTo not validated; adjacent only CVE-2026-58066 (signature wrapping, fixed 8.7.0 via PR #41233), CVE-2026-46423, CVE-2026-45677, CVE-2026-22560, CVE-2020-29594.
findings.conditional_on: the EE saml-enterprise licence with a SAML provider configured, and an IdP that signs assertions for several service providers with one key
findings.impact: High (CVSS 7.4): the SAML validator verifies the signature and the time windows and then trusts the assertion, without ever asking whether it was addressed to this workspace. Audience, SubjectConfirmationData/@Recipient and the response's Destination are never read, and InResponseTo is recorded into the profile but never compared with a request this server sent. Wherever an identity provider signs for several service providers with one key (a Keycloak realm key, an ADFS token-signing certificate, Shibboleth defaults), the operator of any other federated SP, or anyone who captures an assertion inside its validity window, can post it to Rocket.Chat and get a session as its subject, administrators included, with no password and past Rocket.Chat's own login checks.
findings.remediation: In Response.ts refuse a response whose Destination is not this ACS URL, whose assertion Conditions/AudienceRestriction does not name this SP's entity id, and whose SubjectConfirmationData/@Recipient differs from the ACS URL; store the ids of AuthnRequests this server issued and require InResponseTo to match one, accepting unsolicited (IdP-initiated) responses only behind an explicit setting. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/SAML_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (Service Provider considerations and Unsolicited Response considerations) with deploy/knowledge/payloads/PayloadsAllTheThings/SAML Injection/README.md for the test shapes.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps SAML login and removes only the weakness: IdP-initiated logins require an administrator to opt in, and an identity provider configured to omit Audience, Destination or Recipient must be configured to send them (all three are standard and emitted by default by the common IdPs), so a misconfigured federation that worked by accident stops until it is corrected.

findings.title: Account lockout bypass: the per-user failed-login block reads the username as typed, so logins by email or inside a totp envelope are never locked
findings.category: Authentication (account lockout bypass)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (the per-user lock engaged for the username but 15 guesses by email were never blocked and the email form logged in while the username form was locked)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #40195 'Plan: Enhance Login Protection and Fix Email Bypass' (2026-04-17; closed 2026-10-08 with no fix merged): login protection is bypassed when the email address is used. This build still reads only methodArguments[0].user?.username (restrictLoginAttempts.ts:103-106). The totp-envelope leg is not in that report. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/40195
