findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.8): "Block failed login attempts by username" is the documented per-account lockout, and it is decided on the identifier spelling rather than on the account. isValidAttemptByUser reads methodArguments[0].user?.username and returns true when it is absent, which is exactly the shape REST builds for a login by email address ({ email: ... }) and for every attempt carrying a second-factor code ({ totp: { code, login } }). Failures are still counted against the resolved account, so the victim is the one locked out of the username form while the attacker keeps guessing through the email form indefinitely. TOTP verification has no attempt cap of its own either, so an attacker who already has the password can grind six-digit codes under the per-address limits alone.
findings.remediation: Key the per-user decision on the resolved account rather than on the request's spelling: look the account up once (by username, email or whatever identifier the envelope carries, including inside totp.login) and evaluate the block on login.user?._id, or move the decision into the failure and success hooks that already know which account was resolved (restrictLoginAttempts.ts:98-145); and give TOTP failures their own per-account counter and lock instead of TOTPCheck.maxFaildedAttemtpsReached returning false. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (account lockout keyed on the account) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (rate-limit second-factor verification).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the lockout feature and removes only the weakness: failures at email-form logins and inside totp envelopes now count toward the same lock, which is what the setting's name promises, and a TOTP cap can lock out a user who mistypes codes repeatedly, so it should share the existing unlock window and admin unlock path.

findings.title: Password change, reset and remove-other-tokens leave open realtime sessions alive, and an admin-set password is broadcast in clear to them
findings.category: Session management (revocation not applied to the realtime channel; credential in a broadcast)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a stolen token's realtime session survived both a password change and removeOtherTokens, kept reading the victim's private messages, and received the administrator's new password in clear, which then logged in)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-33: searched password change does not log out other websocket sessions; adjacent only CVE-2023-28316 / HackerOne #992280 (sessions surviving 2FA activation, fixed, and enabling 2FA now broadcasts) and PR #41573.
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.5): the remediation a user or administrator performs after a session is stolen does not close the attacker's socket. A DDP connection is disconnected only when a broadcast user diff carries services.resume.loginTokens, and the paths that remove tokens mostly do not broadcast that field: users.removeOtherTokens broadcasts nothing, the profile password change notifies a reduced diff, and Meteor's resetPassword has no hook at all, so the attacker's connection keeps delivering the victim's new messages, mentions and direct-message notifications while REST with the old token is already refused. Worse, when an administrator resets the password through users.update, saveUser broadcasts the data it was given to the user's own channel with the new plaintext password still in it, so the attacker's socket receives the credential the administrator just chose.
findings.remediation: Make every token-removing path announce itself: have the model methods that clear tokens (removeNonLoginTokensExcept, removeNonPATLoginTokensExcept, unsetLoginTokens and the updater in setPasswordUpdater) broadcast the resulting token list (or an explicit forced-logout event for the removed hashes), hook Meteor's reset the same way, and delete password from the diff before notifyOnUserChange in saveUser.ts:365-374. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md (invalidate every session on a credential change; manual session expiration must reach all channels) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md for the broadcast credential.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps realtime delivery and removes only the weakness: a user's other sessions are disconnected when the password changes, when it is reset and when they use remove-other-sessions, which is what the UI already promises; the session performing the change is unaffected, and clients that re-read the user after an admin update now fetch the password-free document (no client displays it).

findings.title: URL-parameter session handoff: ?loginClient=mobile exports the resume token to the rocketchat:// scheme and ?resumeToken= logs the browser into another account
findings.category: Session handoff driven by URL parameters (token export to a custom scheme; login CSRF)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the browser legs need the Playwright drive this stage did not have time to write)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-34: searched loginClient=mobile rocketchat://auth token deep link and resumeToken query login; adjacent only Rocket.Chat.ReactNative PR #7447 (mobile side of the handoff) and PR #41788 (SAML deep link).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.8): two hooks mounted on every page act on bare query parameters that anyone can put in a link. With ?loginClient=mobile or desktop, a logged-in browser reads its stored login token and navigates to rocketchat://auth?host=...&token=<resume token>&userId=..., handing a 90-day session credential (already past the second factor) to whatever program on the device claims that scheme: on Android any app may register it, iOS custom schemes are not exclusive, and desktop handlers are registerable too. With ?resumeToken=<token the attacker owns>, the same page silently logs the victim's browser into the attacker's account, so whatever the victim types next, including files and messages they believe are private, lands in a room the attacker controls.
findings.remediation: Bind the handoff to a flow the native client started: honour loginClient only together with a one-time state value the app generated and the SSO round-tripped, ask the user to confirm the handover, and give the app a single-use code (as loginCode already is) rather than the resume token itself (useShareSessionWithOtherClients.ts:13-33, buildAuthDeeplinkURL.ts:1-5); for the reverse direction, ignore resumeToken when a session already exists or require an explicit confirmation plus a flow-bound nonce (useLoginViaQuery.ts:8-17), and stop putting resume tokens in URLs at all (passportOAuthCallback.ts:47 does the same). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (login CSRF) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Mobile_Application_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (custom URL schemes are not a trusted channel).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the desktop and mobile sign-in handoff and removes only the weakness: the user confirms the handover once per device and the native app receives a single-use code instead of the long-lived token, and a link carrying resumeToken no longer switches an already-signed-in browser (a user who genuinely wants to change account signs out first).

findings.title: Room invite links are not revocable by the room's owners, outlive their creator's rights, and their use limit is not consumed atomically
findings.category: Broken access control (share link not re-validated or revocable)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (the room owner could neither list nor revoke a moderator's permanent link, and the kicked, demoted creator re-entered the private group with it)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-35: searched invite link maxUses race revoke removed member; adjacent only PR #41174 (atomic revoke, 8.7.0), PR #38290, PR #35821.
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.4): an invite link is a bearer capability that nobody in the room can take back. Listing and removing invites check create-invite-links with no room scope, which consults global roles only, so the owners and moderators of a room (whose roles are room-scoped) get not_authorized when they try to revoke their own room's link; only a workspace administrator can, from the global invites page. Redemption re-checks the token's expiry, its use count and the redeemer's ban, but never whether the creator still has any rights in the room, so a link made by a moderator who has since been kicked or demoted keeps letting people (including that moderator) into a private room. And the use count is read-then-incremented unconditionally, so parallel redemptions of a single-use link all pass, while registration in Secret URL mode validates an invite without consuming a use at all.
findings.remediation: Scope the permission to the invite's room in listInvites.ts:11 and removeInvite.ts:12 and surface revocation in the room's own invite panel; on redemption verify the creator still holds create-invite-links in that room (or delete a member's invites when they are kicked, banned or demoted); and consume uses atomically with a conditional update, checking modifiedCount, in both useInviteToken and the Secret URL registration path. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request) and deploy/knowledge/payloads/PayloadsAllTheThings/Race Condition/README.md (limit overrun).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps invite links and removes only the weakness: links created by a member who has since been removed or demoted stop working, room owners gain the ability to revoke, and a single-use link admits exactly one account (so a user who double-submits the join sees one success and one "expired"), while registration through an exhausted link is refused.

findings.title: Mandatory 2FA for a role is enforced only by the web client, so its members keep single-factor access over REST and DDP
findings.category: Security policy enforced client-side only (mandatory MFA)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a member of a role with mandatory two-factor authentication logged in with the password alone over REST and used the role's full access; the policy is read only by the web client)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven on both channels: the policy an administrator switched on is not read by the server at all.
findings.known_evidence: Public since 2019 in the feature's own PR #9748: a user reported the role's mandatory 2FA is bypassed by logging in via mobile, a contributor asked whether it is 'only being enforced at client side level', and Rocket.Chat member sampaiodiego answered 'true'. The 2025 fix PR #37338 changed only client code. No CVE, GHSA or server-side fix; affects 9.1.0-develop at 9f3d6c8c. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/pull/9748
findings.conditional_on: an administrator enabled mandatory 2FA on a role (a security control that is switched on but not enforced server-side)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.8): "Users must use Two Factor Authentication" on a role is a security control an administrator switches on, typically for admin, and it is implemented as a client-side redirect. The only reader of the role's mandatory2fa flag is a React hook that swaps the page for the security settings; on the server, the second-factor check returns true for a user with no enrolled method, whatever their roles say, so a member of that role who never enrolled logs in over REST or DDP and has the role's full access with the password alone. The control's whole purpose is that a stolen password should not be enough for a privileged role, and for every non-web client it is not enforced at all.
findings.remediation: Enforce the flag where sessions are made: in the 2FA onValidateLogin callback (2fa/loginHandler.ts:31-36) and in issueLoginToken, refuse a full session when any of the user's roles carries mandatory2fa and getSecondFactorMethod finds no enrolled method, returning a distinguishable error (totp-setup-required) or a token scoped to the enrolment routes only; keep the client redirect as the user-facing path. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (when MFA is required it is required on every channel) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Verify that Authorization Checks are Performed in the Right Location).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the feature and removes only the weakness: a member of a mandatory-2FA role who has not enrolled can no longer use API clients or the mobile apps until they do (which is the policy's intent), and an integration running as such an account needs a token minted after enrolment, so administrators should enrol service accounts or exclude them from the role before enabling it.

findings.title: Pre-registration squatting survives the owner's OAuth claim: the email meld resets the password but keeps the squatter's sessions and personal access tokens
findings.category: Pre-account takeover (account claim does not purge prior access)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (after the account's real owner claimed it through their identity provider, the earlier squatter's personal access token still read the account, its subscriptions and its direct messages)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: after the owner's provider claim the squatter's token still read the account, its subscriptions and its direct messages.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-37: searched pre-account takeover email meld keeps sessions personal access tokens; adjacent only open PRs #43880 and #43888 (meld password handling) and PR #43840; none mentions sessions or PATs.
findings.conditional_on: an OAuth login provider enabled, with the victim signing in through it after the attacker registered their address
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.8): an attacker registers a future colleague's email address while registration is public (the default), signs in, and mints a personal access token. When the real owner later signs in through an OAuth provider, the email meld links the identity to that existing account and marks the address verified, and the only thing it clears is the password: resetPasswordAndSetRequirePasswordChange unsets services.password and nothing else, so services.resume.loginTokens, where both login tokens and personal access tokens live, survives intact. The attacker keeps reading everything the account receives (direct messages, mentions, the private rooms it joins) and can post as it, from the day the real person starts using the workspace, and the owner's own forced password change does not revoke those tokens because the revocation path requires a bcrypt hash the meld has just removed.
findings.remediation: When the meld links an identity to an account whose address that identity did not verify, purge every credential the previous holder created, not only the password: unset services.resume.loginTokens (login tokens and PATs), the other linked services and any OAuth tokens, alongside the existing services.password unset in accounts_meld.js:22-31; better, stop linking by email without an authenticated session at all (the fix for the OAuth-meld finding), and force a reset when an address is first verified on an account whose password predates that verification. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (account linking requires proof of control of both sides) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Email_Validation_and_Verification_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps social login and removes only the weakness: anyone who pre-created an account and later signs in through the provider loses their earlier sessions and personal access tokens and must create new ones, and silent first-login merging stops for unverified addresses.

findings.title: video-conference.share-chat creates a discussion without the membership and send checks regular discussion creation enforces
findings.category: Broken access control (secondary feature writing into a room; ban and mute bypass)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the route needs a call created by a marketplace video-conference app, which a sealed lab cannot install)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-38: searched video-conference share-chat discussion non-member add-participants; adjacent only PRs #41934 and #41735 (feature design) and PR #43038 (9.0 membership check for discussions in public rooms).
findings.conditional_on: a video-conference provider app installed and a call held in the target room
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.2): conference membership is a separate authorization axis from room membership (canAccessConference admits anyone listed in the call, because participants may legitimately have no access to the room the call started in), and the share-chat discussion branch acts on it without re-checking the room. Its own comment promises "the same rules regular discussion creation enforces", but it checks only the Discussion_enabled switch and start-discussion, which the default user role holds; the real path additionally requires canSendMessageAsync and a status-aware subscription. So an outsider a participant added to the call, or a member the room has banned or muted, creates a discussion under that private room, becomes its owner, pulls in every subscriber of the parent room (which discloses the private membership), and leaves a "started a discussion" notice inside the room they cannot otherwise write to.
findings.remediation: In shareChatWithMembers (service.ts:1857-1870) apply the checks the primary path applies: canSendMessageAsync(rid, caller) and a non-banned, status-aware subscription for the caller, as createDiscussion.ts:99-112 does; refuse once the call has ended (endedAt set); and restrict add-participants to accounts that can access the call's room so conference membership cannot be used to manufacture room access. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request, and do not re-implement a rule partially on a secondary path).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps chat sharing for room members and removes only the weakness: a participant who cannot write in the call's room can no longer move the call's chat into a discussion there (they can still use the call), ended calls no longer allow it, and banned or muted members are refused.

findings.title: Apple identity tokens are replayable across workspaces, because the audience list always includes the shared official iOS app and no nonce is checked
findings.category: Authentication (identity token accepted across relying parties)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the finding needs Apple-signed identity tokens, which a sealed lab cannot obtain or forge)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-39: parent GHSA-c75c-5hc7-j4vp / CVE-2026-55759 (Apple Sign-In skipped aud, exp, nbf, nonce; fixed 8.5.1 and backports) is fixed here (handleIdentityToken.ts:78-100), but the fix always adds DEFAULT_APPLE_AUDIENCES = ['chat.rocket.ios'] and checks no nonce; the cross-workspace replay is not reported.
findings.conditional_on: Apple login enabled (Accounts_OAuth_Apple)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.8): every Rocket.Chat workspace with Apple login accepts an identity token whose audience is chat.rocket.ios, the identifier of the official iOS app, because DEFAULT_APPLE_AUDIENCES is merged into the allowed audiences unconditionally. That identifier is shared by every workspace the app can connect to, so a token the victim's phone produced for workspace A is equally valid at workspace B, and no nonce ties a token to the login attempt that asked for it. Any workspace operator therefore collects replayable credentials from their own users: within the token's lifetime they can log in as those users on any other workspace with Apple login enabled, limited only by whether the victim's account there has an applicable second factor.
findings.remediation: Stop trusting a shared audience and bind the token to the attempt: remove DEFAULT_APPLE_APPLE_AUDIENCES from the merge at handleIdentityToken.ts:95 (make the official app's identifier an explicit per-workspace opt-in setting rather than an implicit default) and require a nonce claim that this server issued for this login, rejecting a token that carries none. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/OAuth2_Cheat_Sheet.md (an identity token is bound to one relying party and one request) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps Apple login and removes only the weakness: a workspace that relies on the official iOS app must list its audience explicitly (a one-line setting change), and app builds that do not send a nonce stop authenticating until they are updated, so the rollout needs the mobile release to land first.

findings.title: Second-factor codes are not single-use: a TOTP code is replayable inside the window and a backup code can be redeemed twice by concurrent requests
findings.category: MFA one-time code replay and consumption race
findings.status: CONFIRMED (the TOTP code was replayed for 4 further sessions; the backup-code race gave 1 token(s))
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-40: searched TOTP code replay backup code race 2FA; adjacent only PR #40734 (TOTP REST migration).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.2): a one-time code stops being one-time. TOTP verification calls speakeasy.verifyDelta with the configured window and records nothing on success, so a code observed after its legitimate use (a shoulder-surfed screen, a screenshot in a ticket, an x-2fa-code header in a proxy log) is accepted again for the remainder of the window, about 90 seconds at the shipped MaxDelta of 1. Backup codes are consumed by loading the array, splicing the matched hash out in memory and writing the whole array back with an unconditional $set, so N concurrent logins presenting the same backup code all find it present, all succeed, and the final write leaves the other codes intact. An attacker with the password turns one glimpsed code into extra sessions and step-ups.
findings.remediation: Record consumption atomically. For TOTP, store services.totp.lastUsedStep and accept a step only through a conditional update that requires lastUsedStep to be lower, so a replay of the same (or an earlier) step fails; for backup codes, consume with updateOne({ _id, 'services.totp.hashedBackup': hash }, { $pull: { 'services.totp.hashedBackup': hash } }) and require modifiedCount === 1 instead of splicing a loaded array and re-setting it (totp.ts:32-44, Users.ts:2326-2337). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (one-time codes must be invalidated on use) with deploy/knowledge/payloads/PayloadsAllTheThings/Race Condition/README.md (limit overrun) for the concurrent half.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps TOTP and backup codes and removes only the weakness: a user who submits the same code twice (a double click, two tabs, a retried request) is told it is invalid the second time and waits for the next code, and a backup code works exactly once.

findings.title: Star privacy is enforced only in the REST serializer, so the message query and the realtime broadcast disclose who starred what
findings.category: Privacy setting bypassed through alternate channels
findings.status: CONFIRMED (one member read another member's private stars: the query filter returned exactly the starred message, and the realtime broadcast carried the raw starred array)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-41: searched starred messages visible to other users starredIds stream privacy; adjacent only HackerOne #1060837 (writing stars on arbitrary messages), issue #20099, CVE-2026-106075 (fixed 9.0.0).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): Rocket.Chat presents stars as private ("only you have access to your stars") and enforces that in one place, the REST serializer, which trims each message's starred array to the caller's own entry. Two other paths ignore it. The room message routes (channels.messages, groups.messages, im.messages) build their Mongo filter from a client-supplied starredIds list and select on starred._id before the serializer runs, so a caller can ask "which messages in this room did this colleague star" and read the answer from the result set. And the realtime copy prepared for stream-room-messages drops hidden messages and private author fields but keeps starred in full, so every subscriber of a room sees the complete star list each time a message changes. Bookmark activity (interest in a job posting, an HR notice, a particular incident) is personal information the product promised not to share.
findings.remediation: Apply the rule where the data is selected and where it is emitted, not only where it is serialized: accept starredIds only when it names the caller (or drop the parameter in favour of chat.getStarredMessages) in channels.ts:517, groups.ts:1210 and im.ts:659, and either remove starred from the payload getMessageToBroadcast returns (notifyListener.ts:443-470) or apply the per-subscriber filterStarred at emit time. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request, including on queries and on realtime pushes) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/User_Privacy_Protection_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps stars and removes only the weakness: filtering a room's messages by another user's stars stops working (no first-party client does it, and the caller's own stars remain filterable), and clients learn their own star state from the REST response rather than from the shared array in a broadcast.

findings.title: Attacker-chosen text in the workspace's own registration and reset emails, sent to any address
findings.category: Trusted platform email carrying attacker-controlled text
findings.status: CONFIRMED (the workspace sent its own genuine mail, from its own address, to a third party's mailbox carrying a sentence the attacker chose)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-42: searched registration email name hyperlink injection; adjacent only HackerOne #833470 'HTML Injection into Email via Signup' (markup, refused today by validateNameChars.ts:6), PR #11644, issue #35965, CVE-2026-65644. The plain-text and auto-link variant is not reported.
findings.impact: Medium by CVSS (4.3), realistically Low: an unauthenticated caller registers with somebody else's email address and a display name that is really a sentence, and the workspace sends that person its own genuine verification mail, from its own address, with the attacker's text in the greeting. The same name reaches the password-reset mail's subject and body, there inserted with no escaping and no dot-neutralisation at all. Name validation refuses only <, >, \ and /, so markup is blocked but sentences, phone numbers and bare domains (which mail clients auto-link) pass. The result is phishing content carried by mail that passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the organisation, which is exactly the trust that makes it effective; no markup and no credential theft happen directly, which is why the realistic severity is lower than the band.
findings.remediation: Do not put an unverified registrant's display name into mail sent to an address they have not proven they own: greet by the address (or by nothing) in verifyEmail until the address is verified, and pass the name through safeHtmlDots and HTML escaping in the reset template as the verification template already half-does (startup.js:104-141). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Email_Validation_and_Verification_Cheat_Sheet.md (ownership verification before acting on an address) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.md for not reflecting unvalidated input into trusted output.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps both mails and removes only the weakness: the greeting shows the address rather than the registrant's chosen name until the address is verified, so a legitimate new user sees a slightly less personal first email, and the reset mail renders a name containing dots as text.

findings.title: OAuth login skips the second factor for any account inside the registration grace window, even one that has enrolled TOTP
findings.category: MFA skipped on an alternate login path (registration grace window)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an account with TOTP enrolled was signed in through OAuth with no second factor, inside the registration grace window, while its password login still demanded the code)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: an account with TOTP enrolled was signed in through OAuth with no factor inside the registration window.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-43: searched OAuth login skips 2FA newly registered account remember window; adjacent only issue #41394 (SAML 2FA with unverified email), PR #42099, PR #43029.
findings.conditional_on: an OAuth login provider enabled
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.2): the registration grace window exists so that a brand-new account with no second factor yet can finish setting the workspace up, and the step-up path implements it correctly, granting the grace only when the user has no 2FA method at all. The OAuth decision function re-implements the same idea and drops that condition: doesUserRequire2FA returns false for every account younger than Accounts_TwoFactorAuthentication_RememberFor (1800 seconds by default) before it ever looks for an enrolled method. So for 30 minutes after an account is created, an OAuth login completes with no second factor even though the owner has already enrolled TOTP, while a password login for the same account at the same instant demands the code.
findings.remediation: Evaluate the method first and apply the grace only when there is none, exactly as the step-up path does at 2fa/code/index.ts:102-110: in doesUserRequire2FA (twoFactorAuth.ts:23-41), call getSecondFactorMethod(user) before the remember-window test and return it whenever a method exists. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (once a factor is enrolled it applies to every authentication path) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the grace for brand-new accounts that have not enrolled anything (so the setup wizard and first-run flows still work) and removes only the weakness: an account that enrolled a method inside its first 30 minutes is asked for it at its next OAuth login, which is what its owner expects.

findings.title: CAS session fixation: the credential token is chosen in the service URL, so a crafted link to the real CAS server hands the victim's account to the attacker
findings.category: Authentication bypass (session fixation in the SSO handoff)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the CAS handshake needs a trusted CAS server over HTTPS, which this sealed lab cannot provide)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-44: searched CAS login credentialToken session fixation service URL; adjacent only GHSA-rr54-jf4h-6cj9 / CVE-2026-45688 (NoSQL injection hijacking in-flight CAS and SAML logins, fixed 8.5.0), CVE-2022-35248 (2FA bypass by asking for CAS, fixed), open PR #40196.
findings.conditional_on: CAS_enabled with CAS_base_url and CAS_login_url pointing at the organisation's CAS server
findings.impact: High (CVSS 8.1): the token that becomes a Rocket.Chat session is picked by whoever builds the CAS service URL, and anyone who knows it can redeem it. The client draws a random credentialToken and embeds it in the service URL as /_cas/<token>; the server validates the returned ticket against that same URL and stores the validated identity under the token from the request path; login({ cas: { credentialToken } }) then hands a full session to any caller presenting it within 60 seconds. Nothing binds the completed round trip to the browser that started it. So an attacker who picks their own token, sends the victim a link to the organisation's genuine CAS server with that token in the service parameter, and polls the login method, receives the victim's account, administrators included, with no password and with CAS explicitly exempted from Rocket.Chat's second factor.
findings.remediation: Make the token the server's and bind it to one browser: generate it when the popup opens and pair it with a secret delivered only to that browser (an HttpOnly cookie scoped to /_cas, or a credentialSecret returned to the opener as Meteor's own OAuth flow does), and require both at login({ cas }); accept only serviceValidate (refuse proxy tickets unless allow-listed); and remove the cas exemption from the 2FA callback (2fa/loginHandler.ts:18-27) unless MFA is explicitly delegated to the identity provider. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/wstg/document/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/06-Session_Management_Testing/03-Testing_for_Session_Fixation.md and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (login CSRF).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps CAS login and removes only the weakness: a CAS login completed in a different browser from the one that started it stops working (no first-party client does that), CAS users who have a Rocket.Chat second factor are asked for it unless MFA is delegated, and proxy tickets are refused unless allow-listed.

findings.title: Profanity filter is a per-token, per-word regex scan on the request path, so one member stalls the whole server for seconds per message
findings.category: Denial of service (inefficient algorithmic complexity on the request path)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (one member's 500-token message took 3.32s of server time with the filter on against 0.31s with it off, and a bystander waited up to 2.78s)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: one member's message cost ten times what the same message costs with the filter off, and a bystander waited with it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-45: searched bad-words clean slow performance denial of service; OSV bad-words@3.0.4 and badwords-list@1.0.0: 0; only competing-library benchmarks exist.
findings.conditional_on: Message_AllowBadWordsFilter (the profanity filter) enabled
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.5): with the profanity filter on, every message is passed synchronously through bad-words' clean() before the markdown parse, on the single thread that serves every other request. The bundled library splits the text on word boundaries and, for each token, compiles and tests a fresh regular expression for each of its roughly 900 built-in words plus the administrator's list, so the cost is the product of token count and list size. Stage 05 measured it in this build: about 3.96 s for 5000 characters of prose and about 8.9 s for a 5000-character message of single letters. During that time the workspace serves nothing: no REST, no DDP, no stream delivery. An ordinary member repeating such messages at the shipped send rate keeps the server saturated, and ordinary long messages cost seconds each even without an attacker.
findings.remediation: Build one combined, escaped alternation (extending the existing badWordsRegex field in BeforeSaveBadWords.ts, which already does a single-pass replace for the administrator's list) when the settings change, and replace matches in one pass over the message instead of calling the library's per-token clean(); optionally run the filter off the event loop with a time budget and fall back to the unfiltered text. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Denial_of_Service_Cheat_Sheet.md (bound the work one request may do; never let a single request monopolise a shared thread).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the filter and both word lists and removes only the weakness: a few edge cases where the library's per-token matching and a single combined pattern disagree may mask slightly differently, and administrator-supplied words are treated as literals rather than as regular expressions.

findings.title: Anonymous write into any room through livechat/page.visited, which resolves neither the visitor token nor the room
findings.category: Missing authorization (anonymous write into arbitrary rooms; content spoofing)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an unauthenticated caller wrote an attacker-chosen notice into #general through livechat/page.visited, attributed to the workspace bot, and the write still lands (hidden) with the notice setting off)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-46: searched livechat page.visited navigation history any room unauthenticated; adjacent only PR #14970 (2019, removed the visitor and room validation, the origin of the gap), PR #10091, PR #42710, CVE-2021-48022.
findings.conditional_on: Livechat_Visitor_navigation_as_a_message enabled (with it off, the same request still writes a hidden message into any room)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.3): the Livechat page-tracking endpoint takes a visitor token and a room id from an unauthenticated request and passes them to savePageHistory, which never looks the visitor up and never loads the room: it just saves a system message into the room id it was given, authored by rocket.cat, with the title and URL the caller supplied. With Livechat_Visitor_navigation_as_a_message enabled, that notice is visible, so anyone on the internet posts bot-attributed, system-styled text and links into #general or any room whose id they hold. With the setting at its shipped off, the same request still writes the document into that room marked _hidden, which bumps the room's counters and lands in exports and in the routes elsewhere in this report that return hidden messages.
findings.remediation: Resolve the visitor from the token and require rid to be that visitor's own open Omnichannel room, exactly as the sibling livechat/upload route does with LivechatRooms.findOneOpenByRoomIdAndVisitorToken (upload.ts:31-34); refuse the route while Livechat_enabled is false; and store pre-room navigation with no room id rather than with a caller-supplied one (tracking.ts:9-54). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (resolve the object inside what the caller owns).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps navigation history for real visitor conversations and removes only the weakness: a tracking call naming another room, a non-Omnichannel room or an unknown visitor is refused, and the endpoint writes nothing while Omnichannel is off.

findings.title: channels.anonymousread serves Omnichannel conversations and hidden messages to unauthenticated callers, and getRoomRoles skips its access check for them
findings.category: Broken access control (anonymous read of Omnichannel rooms and hidden messages)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an unauthenticated caller read a customer support conversation and a deleted message through channels.anonymousread; the role-listing leg is not reachable, every entry point to it requires authentication)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-47: parents fixed here: the 7.11.0 'Broken Access Control in AnonymousRead' hotfix (#36982) and CVE-2022-35247 (getRoomRoles ACL, HackerOne #1447440), whose check skips anonymous callers; the Livechat-room and hidden-message legs are not reported.
findings.conditional_on: Accounts_AllowAnonymousRead enabled (main leg also needs Omnichannel in use)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.9): with anonymous read enabled, the route meant to expose public channels exposes more than that. Its lookup, findChannelByIdOrName, admits rooms of type l (Omnichannel), so a Livechat conversation id returns the whole customer conversation to a caller with no session; the handler checks only the setting and a private-team special case rather than calling canAccessRoomAsync, and its query is { rid } with no _hidden filter, so hidden messages of public channels (which other findings here show include deleted and edited-away content) come back too. Separately, getRoomRoles runs its CVE-2022-35247 access check only when a user is present, so an anonymous DDP caller gets the owners, moderators and leaders of any room by id, and getRoomByTypeAndName likewise skips its check and its lastMessage redaction for anonymous callers.
findings.remediation: Make the anonymous path use the shared validator rather than a partial re-implementation: in channels.anonymousread (channels.ts:2092-2123) accept only t 'c', call canAccessRoomAsync(findResult, this.user), which already handles anonymous callers and private teams, and add _hidden: { $ne: true } to the query; in getRoomRoles.ts:26 and publications/room/index.ts:81-93 run the same validator for anonymous callers instead of gating it on fromUser. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default; Validate the Permissions on Every Request).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps anonymous reading of public channels, which is what the setting is for, and removes only the weakness: Omnichannel conversations, hidden messages, private rooms' role lists and channels inside private teams are no longer served to callers without a session.

findings.title: Omnichannel external frame puts the agent's plaintext session token in the frame URL, and the encryption key the setting promises is a public setting
findings.category: Sensitive data exposure (session token in a URL; documented encryption not applied)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the agent-side browser drive did not fit this stage's time budget; the settings themselves are checked here)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-48: searched Omnichannel external frame token URL and the public JWK setting; adjacent only open PRs #43847 and #43848 (React rewrite of the container).
findings.conditional_on: Omnichannel_External_Frame_Enabled with Omnichannel_External_Frame_URL and _Encryption_JWK set
findings.impact: High (CVSS 7.4): the external-frame feature embeds a third-party CRM page beside a Livechat conversation, and the product's setting pair (a frame URL plus an encryption JWK) tells the operator the agent's token will be encrypted. The component does encrypt it, and then discards the result: the ciphertext is used only as a readiness flag in the memo's dependency list, while the URL receives frameURL.searchParams.append('t', authToken), the plaintext session token. That token is a 90-day credential already past any second factor, and it is now in a URL handed to an external host, so it lands in that host's access logs, in proxies and CDNs on the way, in Referer headers, in browser history and in any analytics or extension code running on the CRM page. Separately, the JWK that should have protected it is registered public: true, so every client (including an unauthenticated one through settings.public) can read it, making server-side encryption with that key worthless as well.
findings.remediation: Append token.data, the ciphertext, as t and never authToken (ExternalFrameContainer.tsx:27-38), and register Omnichannel_External_Frame_Encryption_JWK with public: false so the key stays server-side, moving the encryption to the server; better still, mint a short-lived, single-purpose frame token and deliver it by postMessage to the frame's exact origin rather than putting any credential in a URL. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md (never transmit a session identifier in a URL) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/wstg/document/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/06-Session_Management_Testing/04-Testing_for_Exposed_Session_Variables.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the feature and removes only the weakness: an external system that consumed the plaintext t must decrypt it, which is what the setting already documents, and the key is no longer readable by browsers, so any integration that decrypted client-side must move that step server-side.

findings.title: With message edit history on, deleted and edited-away content stays readable: personal exports include the hidden copies and their files, and chat.getMessage returns them by id
findings.category: Sensitive data exposure (soft-deleted content served to members)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a member read an edited-away secret and a deleted message's text through chat.getMessage, which the room's own history withholds)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-49: searched Message_KeepHistory deleted messages included in data export getMessage hidden; adjacent only PR #43364 and CVE-2023-28318 / HackerOne #1379451.
findings.conditional_on: Message_KeepHistory (keep per-message editing history) enabled
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): when Message_KeepHistory is enabled, deleting a message does not delete it. The delete path either clones the message as a hidden document or marks the original _hidden, and marks its uploads _hidden rather than removing them; editing likewise stores the previous version as a hidden document in the same room. The lists, sync and search routes do filter hidden messages, so the content disappears from the client, which is what makes the gap convincing: the personal data export queries the room by id with an empty filter and writes every document and every file it finds, and chat.getMessage loads a message by id with no hidden condition and returns it to any member of the room. So a member (including one who joined after the deletion) extracts credentials pasted by mistake, personal data and moderated content that the client told the author could not be recovered.
findings.remediation: Honour the soft-delete marker on the paths that bypass it: add _hidden: { $ne: true } (and exclude the parent history copies) to the export query in exportRoomMessagesToFile.ts:217-219, which is called with an empty filter from processDataDownloads.ts:186-194, and to the lookup in getSingleMessage.ts:8; refuse hidden uploads on the file route unless the caller holds an administrative permission; and if edit history is meant for audit, expose it behind view-room-administration rather than to every member. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default; Validate the Permissions on Every Request) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/User_Privacy_Protection_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps edit history for administrators and compliance tooling and removes only the weakness: members' exports, chat.getMessage and direct file links stop returning deleted messages, earlier versions and deleted files, which the client already hides, so a user who relied on the export as an archive of their own deleted drafts loses that.

findings.title: Slack bridge binds channels and users by name, so a Slack member posts into a same-named private group as a same-named local user
findings.category: Broken access control (room and identity binding by a user-controlled name)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the Slack bridge needs a real Slack workspace and outbound access, neither available in a sealed lab)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-50: searched Slack bridge private group same name channel mapping security; adjacent only functional name-mapping issues #22218, #28400, #11854, #15361 and the #14273 fix.
findings.conditional_on: SlackBridge_Enabled with a Slack bot token (read leg also SlackBridge_Out_Enabled and SlackBridge_Out_All)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.8): the bridge decides which local room a Slack channel is and which local account a Slack user is by matching names it does not control. An unknown Slack channel is bound to whatever local room shares its name, of any type, so creating a Slack channel called after a private group links the two; an unknown Slack user is bound to the local account with the same email address or, failing that, the same username (bots by username alone), so a Slack bot named admin is attributed to the workspace's administrator. The relay then posts through the library sendMessage, which performs no membership or permission check of its own. A member of the bridged Slack workspace therefore injects messages into Rocket.Chat private groups as colliding local users, and with the broad outbound relay enabled receives those groups' traffic in Slack.
findings.remediation: Link only what an administrator mapped: in RocketAdapter.ts bind a Slack channel to a local room through an explicit mapping (refusing p and d rooms unless mapped), link a Slack user only to an account an administrator or that user confirmed (creating a separate bridged account otherwise, never matching on username for bots), and call canSendMessageAsync for the mapped account before relaying a message. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (resolve objects through what the caller owns, not through an attacker-chosen key) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps bridging and removes only the weakness: administrators map channels explicitly, Slack users who share a handle with a local account appear as separate bridged accounts rather than being merged, and a bridged post into a room the mapped account may not write to is dropped; existing mappings keep working because they are stored as import ids.

findings.title: Livechat transcript relays visitor-written HTML from the workspace's own mail address to any recipient the caller names
findings.category: HTML injection into outbound email (trusted-sender relay)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an anonymous visitor made the workspace mail attacker-authored HTML, with a working phishing link, from its own address to a third party; the same markup as message text is escaped, so the upload description is the sink)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #42432 'escapeHtml result discarded in sendTranscript leaving attachment description unescaped' (open, 2026-09-29) and fix PR #42433 (open, unmerged); sendTranscript.ts:164 unchanged at 9f3d6c8c. The caller-chosen recipient and the unenforced Livechat_enable_transcript are not in that report. PR #36016 (transcript hotfix) escapes message text only. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/42432
findings.conditional_on: Livechat_enabled (Omnichannel on) with a room that can be opened
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.7): the anonymous transcript route takes the recipient address from the request body, and sendTranscript builds the mail body by interpolating a message's first attachment description into HTML with the escaping discarded: the code computes escapeHtml(messageContent) and throws the result away, then inserts the raw description. A visitor (anyone, since visitor registration is anonymous) uploads a file whose description is markup, then asks for the transcript to be sent to any address. The result is arbitrary HTML delivered by the organisation's own mail server, from its own sender address, so SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass. The route also never checks Livechat_enable_transcript, so the workspace sends transcripts even where the operator disabled them, and the recipient need not be the address on the visitor's record.
findings.remediation: Assign the escaped value (messageContent = escapeHtml(message.attachments[0].description || '')) and escape every interpolated field in sendTranscript.ts:158-176; in the transcript route, enforce Livechat_enable_transcript, send a visitor-requested transcript only to the address stored on that visitor or contact rather than to one supplied in the body, and cap the number of transcript requests per room. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (output encoding for the HTML context, applied to every interpolated value) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Email_Validation_and_Verification_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps transcripts and removes only the weakness: markup typed into an attachment description appears as text in the mail, a visitor can no longer choose an arbitrary recipient (the stored address is used), and the route refuses while the workspace has transcripts disabled.

findings.title: Smarsh compliance export interpolates message text and sender names into the archived HTML unescaped, so a member forges or hides archive entries
findings.category: Integrity of compliance records (HTML injection into archived email)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the Smarsh compliance export is a licensed enterprise module and is not present on this workspace)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-52: searched Smarsh connector HTML injection compliance archive; adjacent only PR #4130 (the connector) and HackerOne #3779690 (HTML room export XSS).
findings.conditional_on: Smarsh_Enabled with Smarsh_Email set
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 5.4): the Smarsh connector builds the regulatory archive as an HTML table and pushes raw values into it: rows.push(message.msg) for the text and rows.push(`${sender.name} <...>`) for the author, with no escaping, and the table is mailed as the HTML body to the archive address. A member who posts table markup therefore writes rows of their own into the record (attributed to whomever they like, with any timestamp) and, by opening an HTML comment, hides the genuine rows that follow. Separately, the loop returns out of the whole job when a message's author no longer exists, so one message from a deleted user stops archiving for every room processed after it. The archive is what an organisation produces to a regulator, so its integrity is the point of the feature.
findings.remediation: Escape every interpolated value in generateEml.ts (the message text at :110-114 and the sender name at :78-82, through escapeHTML as the surrounding code already does for the angle brackets) and replace the return at :71 with continue, falling back to message.u.username when the author record is gone so a deleted user cannot halt the export. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (output encoding for the HTML context) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.md (never let logged content alter the record's structure).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps the export and removes only the weakness: markup typed in a message is archived as literal text, exactly as the chat client displays it, and a message whose author has been deleted is archived under the stored username instead of ending the run.

findings.title: IRC bridge mirrors every room, private groups included, to the IRC network and joins any IRC user into the local room of the same name
findings.category: Exposure of private rooms to an external network
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the IRC bridge needs an IRC server to peer with, which this sealed lab does not provide)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-53: searched IRC bridge private rooms relayed join channel; no report. The vendor's setting alert ('IRC support is a work in progress. Use on a production system is not recommended at this time.') and the bridge README warn against production use.
findings.conditional_on: IRC_Enabled with a linked IRC server (the vendor marks the bridge not for production)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 6.5): the bridge treats the IRC side as a peer with the same rights as the workspace. onSaveMessage relays every saved message in a non-direct room to #<room name> on IRC, with no distinction between public channels and private groups, so a private group's traffic is published to the IRC network as it is written. In the other direction, a peer JOIN resolves the local room with Rooms.findOneByName and calls addUserToRoom with no room-type or permission check (creating a public channel if none exists), and a peer PRIVMSG resolves the room the same way and posts through the library sendMessage, which performs no authorization. An IRC user who joins a channel named after a private group therefore reads it and writes into it, with no Rocket.Chat account. The vendor marks the bridge not recommended for production, which is why a human must decide whether this is a vulnerability or an unsupported feature.
findings.remediation: Relay only rooms an administrator mapped (public channels by default), never p or d rooms, in onSaveMessage.js:29-36; in joinedChannel.js and sentMessage.js resolve the room through that mapping rather than by name, add an IRC account to a mapped public channel only after canAccessRoom, and require membership before accepting a PRIVMSG. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (never resolve an object by a name the other side controls).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps IRC bridging of the channels an administrator chooses and removes only the weakness: private groups and direct messages stop being relayed, IRC users can join only mapped public channels, and a peer message naming an unmapped room is dropped, so a deployment that relied on implicit name mirroring must declare its mappings.

findings.title: Omnichannel offline form mails visitor fields unescaped to the support mailbox, and the host field lands inside an href
findings.category: HTML injection into staff email (content spoofing)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an anonymous form submission delivered attacker-authored HTML and an attacker-chosen link into the support mailbox from the workspace's own address)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; unauthenticated, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-54: searched livechat offline message email HTML injection; adjacent only CVE-2026-65644 (HackerOne #3872858, visitor name in the agent UI, fixed 8.8.0), PR #3147, HackerOne #833470.
findings.conditional_on: an offline message recipient configured (Livechat_offline_email or a department email)
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.7): the offline form is the anonymous "nobody is available, leave a message" box on the Livechat widget, and sendOfflineMessage builds its notification mail by concatenating the visitor's name, email address and message into HTML with no encoding, plus the host field directly inside an href attribute with no scheme check. The mail goes from the workspace's own From_Email to the configured support mailbox, so staff receive attacker-authored markup and links in a message their own system sent, with the organisation's SPF, DKIM and DMARC behind it. With message forwarding enabled, the same unescaped text is also posted into an internal channel as rocket.cat, so the content lands in the workspace too, attributed to the platform's bot.
findings.remediation: HTML-escape name, email, message and host in messages.ts:39-48, accept host only when it parses as an http(s) URL before putting it in an href (or drop the link and show the text), and in offlineMessageToChannel.ts post the visitor's text as a quoted attachment with markdown and mentions disabled rather than concatenating it into the message body. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md (output encoding per context, including URL attributes) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Unvalidated_Redirects_and_Forwards_Cheat_Sheet.md for the href.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps offline messages and removes only the weakness: markup and links a visitor types appear as literal text in the staff mail and in the forwarded channel message, and a host value that is not an http(s) URL is shown as text instead of being linked.

findings.title: Missing permission check on retentionOverrideGlobal lets any room owner exempt their room from the retention policy
findings.category: Missing authorization on a compliance setting
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an ordinary room owner exempted its own room from the workspace retention policy, while the sibling retention field on the same route refused it)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: PR #43383 by a Rocket.Chat member (merged 2026-11-10; its tests are in this build at saveRoomSettings.test.ts:461-467): 'retentionOverrideGlobal has no permission check on the server. Only the UI hides it. Unit and API tests pin this behavior', and 'This PR does not change them'. No fix, no advisory. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/pull/43383
findings.conditional_on: RetentionPolicy_Enabled for the room's type
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): every other per-room retention field in saveRoomSettings has a validator that refuses a caller without edit-room-retention-policy in the room; retentionOverrideGlobal has a saver and no validator, so the only gate it inherits is edit-room, which owners and moderators hold (and any user becomes an owner by creating a channel). Setting it to true is enough: the prune job's global pass selects rooms with retention.overrideGlobal not true, so the room is skipped, and the per-room pass only takes rooms whose own retention.enabled is set, which the owner cannot set without the permission. The room's messages therefore escape the deletion schedule the organisation mandated, quietly: nothing audits the change and the UI does not show the field to users who lack the permission.
findings.remediation: Add a retentionOverrideGlobal entry to the validator table in saveRoomSettings.ts that refuses unless the caller holds edit-room-retention-policy in the room (or the submitted value equals the stored one), exactly as retentionMaxAge, retentionExcludePinned, retentionFilesOnly and retentionIgnoreThreads already do at :185-237. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default: a field without an explicit rule must not default to the weaker one).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps per-room retention control for holders of edit-room-retention-policy and removes only the weakness: an owner without that permission can no longer set the override, which is what the UI already implies, so a workspace that silently relied on owners setting it must grant the permission explicitly.

findings.title: postMessage command channels accept any origin: iframe login never checks it, and the iframe integration ships with origin *
findings.category: Origin validation error (cross-window command injection)
findings.status: NEEDS_MANUAL (the two-document browser drive did not fit this stage's time budget; the shipped origin settings are checked here)
findings.confidence_reasoning: The mechanism is clear in source; the lab could not complete the trigger, so a person has to finish it.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-56: searched iframe login postMessage login-with-token origin check; adjacent only open issue #42490 (IframeModal listener without checks, a different listener) and issue #9530 (2018); the docs describe the * default.
findings.conditional_on: Accounts_iframe_enabled, or Iframe_Integration_receive_enable with its origin left at the shipped *
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): both embedding features listen for window messages and act on them without establishing who sent them. The iframe-login listener checks only that the message data is an object and then switches on data.event, so any window holding a reference to the workspace tab can send login-with-token and move that tab into an account of the attacker's choosing, or trigger try-iframe-login. The iframe-integration listener does compare origins, but skips the comparison when Iframe_Integration_receive_origin is *, which is the value the setting ships with, so enabling the feature without editing that field accepts commands from everywhere: logout, go to a room, and the rest of the command table. One click on an attacker page (window.open plus a postMessage) is enough, and a victim who does not notice the account switch keeps typing into rooms the attacker controls.
findings.remediation: Establish the sender before acting: in useIframeLoginListener.ts:21-26 and useIframeCommands.ts:112-120 require event.source === window.parent and event.origin to be on a non-wildcard allow-list, and ship Iframe_Integration_receive_origin empty (general.ts:316) so enabling the feature without configuring an origin accepts nothing rather than everything. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/HTML5_Security_Cheat_Sheet.md (Web Messaging: always verify the origin and, where possible, the source of a received message).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps both embedding features and removes only the weakness: a portal must list its origin explicitly before its commands are honoured, and commands from opener windows (as opposed to the embedding parent) are refused, so an integration that relied on the wildcard must set its origin.

findings.title: statistics.telemetry lets any signed-in user increment any numeric workspace setting, weakening 2FA, lockouts and rate limits
findings.category: Missing function-level authorization (settings write via telemetry)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an ordinary account raised Accounts_TwoFactorAuthentication_MaxDelta from 1 to 121 through statistics.telemetry, and the widened window then accepted a 20-minute-old TOTP code that the shipped value refuses)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run: an ordinary account raised a security setting and the widened window then accepted a stale TOTP code; one allow-list fixes it.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #42484 'statistics.telemetry lets any logged-in user $inc arbitrary settings' (2026-10-01; closed 2026-10-02 by the vendor, 'we will track it'), same handler and root cause; updateStatsCounter.ts:8-15 unchanged at 9f3d6c8c. No CVE or GHSA. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/42484
findings.impact: High (CVSS 8.1): the telemetry endpoint needs only authentication and dispatches each submitted event by name; the registered updateCounter handler calls Settings.incrementValueById(data.settingsId, 1) on whatever id the caller supplies, filtered only by the setting not being blocked. Stage 06 counted 109 writable numeric settings in the shipped configuration, so the lowest role can raise Accounts_TwoFactorAuthentication_MaxDelta until most random TOTP codes verify, lift the failed-login thresholds and the email-code attempt cap, raise Message_MaxAllowedSize to widen the parser denial-of-service findings, or, in the other direction, raise the password minimum length and the unblock times until nobody can register, reset a password or log in after a single mistake. The change is applied through the settings store and broadcast as a normal setting change, with no entry in the settings audit trail, and the body schema sets no maxItems, so one request can carry thousands of increments.
findings.remediation: Restrict the handler to the counters it exists for: in updateStatsCounter.ts accept only the fixed set of hidden statistics counter ids the client actually sends (or move those counters into their own collection, out of the settings store), and add maxItems to params in the telemetry schema (statistics.ts:57-73) so a single request cannot carry an unbounded number of increments. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Deny by Default; Enforce Least Privileges) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Mass_Assignment_Cheat_Sheet.md (allow-list the fields a request may address).
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps telemetry and removes only the weakness: the handful of counters the first-party client reports keep working, and any other settings id is refused, which no shipped client sends; a deployment with a custom client that incremented other settings through this path must use the settings API with a permission instead.

findings.title: Mass assignment in teams.create: the caller's room.extraData is spread into the new room, setting default, featured and other administrative flags
findings.category: Mass assignment
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an ordinary account created a room flagged default and featured for the whole workspace, which a new account then joined automatically)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-58: parent HackerOne #1132202 (createRoom extraData override) was fixed by closing extraData on channels.create and groups.create only; PR #42053 notes the team path spreads room.extraData verbatim. Adjacent CVE-2026-72919 (channels.convertToTeam).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): the teams.create body declares room as an open object, the team service strips only abacAttributes and options, and createRoom spreads the rest of extraData into the stored room document. So any user who may create a team (the default user role) sets room fields that belong to room administration: default: true makes every newly registered account a member of that room without an invitation, featured: true places it in the directory's featured list, and the retention and system-message fields are equally reachable. The sibling create routes close the same object with a comment naming exactly these fields, so the intended rule exists and this path misses it. The practical result is a private room, named to look official, that every newcomer silently joins and that the attacker runs.
findings.remediation: Close the schema the way ChannelsCreateProps does: give room in TeamsCreateProps.ts:23-25 explicit properties (readOnly and an extraData limited to topic, broadcast and encrypted) with additionalProperties: false, or have Team.create pass only those keys through to Room.create rather than spreading roomProps and roomExtraData. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Mass_Assignment_Cheat_Sheet.md (bind an explicit, minimal set of fields) with deploy/knowledge/payloads/PayloadsAllTheThings/Mass Assignment/README.md for the probe shapes.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps team creation and removes only the weakness: an API client that set other room fields at creation receives a 400 and must use rooms.saveRoomSettings afterwards, where the per-field permission checks apply; the web client's own create flow sends only the permitted fields.

findings.title: chat.syncThreadsList returns the hidden full copy of a deleted thread root, so members read deleted content on a default install
findings.category: Deleted data exposure (missing response filtering)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a member read the full text of a deleted message through the thread catch-up route, which its non-sync sibling withholds)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, default configuration.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-59: open vendor PR #43343 'thread sync returns the content of deleted messages' covers only the trash-based remove list (unfixed here); this finding's hidden history copy in the update list is a different path. Also CVE-2026-65645 (DDP getThreadsList injection, fixed 8.8.0).
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): deleting a message that started a thread always keeps a copy, whatever the workspace's history setting says, because deleteMessage computes keepHistory as the setting OR "this is a thread root"; the clone carries every field of the original, its text and its files, marked _hidden with a fresh _updatedAt. chat.syncThreadsList then selects thread roots by rid and tcount with only an _updatedAt bound and returns the raw documents, with no _hidden filter and no per-user normalisation, while its paginated twin chat.getThreadsList does filter them. So in the shipped configuration any member can ask for threads updated since a time before a deletion and read the deleted message's original text, its attachment references, and the other members' star lists that normalisation would have removed.
findings.remediation: Add _hidden: { $ne: true } to the update queries of chat.syncThreadsList (chat.ts:1212-1221) and chat.syncThreadMessages, as chat.getThreadsList already does at chat.ts:1140-1141, and pass the results through normalizeMessagesForUser so private per-user fields are filtered as on every other message route. Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.md (Validate the Permissions on Every Request) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/User_Privacy_Protection_Cheat_Sheet.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps thread synchronisation and removes only the weakness: clients stop receiving hidden history documents (no first-party client renders them) and stop receiving other members' star arrays, so a client that displayed a deleted thread root from its cache will show the "message removed" stub instead.

findings.title: Meteor's resetPassword and changePassword set any password: the policy is enforced in the browser and on one REST path only
findings.category: Client-side enforcement (alternate channel missing checks)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (a one-character password was accepted through the method bridge and then logged in, on a workspace whose policy demands fourteen characters, and the change switch is not read there either)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven: a one-character password was accepted and then logged in on a workspace that requires fourteen.
findings.known_evidence: Issue #9434 '[BUG] Disabled password change bypass via forgot password' (opened 2018-01-17 by a Rocket.Chat member, still open) is the Accounts_AllowPasswordChange leg; this build still sets passwords through Meteor's methods without Rocket.Chat's checks. The policy leg has no public report; open PR #43199 fixes the sibling gap on users.create only. https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/issues/9434
findings.impact: Medium (CVSS 4.3): Rocket.Chat's password rules (minimum length and composition, the no-reuse history, the Accounts_AllowPasswordChange switch and the second-factor step-up) live in its own REST path, saveUserProfile, and in the browser. Meteor's original accounts-password methods are still registered and still set passwords, and both are reachable from outside the browser through the method bridges (method.call for changePassword, method.callAnon for resetPassword) as well as over DDP. The reset page itself calls the Meteor method directly after validating in the client, so a caller who skips the page sets a one-character password on any account whose reset token they hold, and a signed-in user changes their own password to anything, including when an administrator has switched password changes off entirely.
findings.remediation: Put the rules behind the method, not beside it: replace Meteor's changePassword handler with one that applies Accounts_AllowPasswordChange, the history check, passwordPolicy.validate and the second-factor step-up (or remove it, since no shipped client calls it), and validate the policy and history before Meteor's resetPassword completes, or have the reset page post to a REST route that already does (saveUserProfile.ts:61-76 is the reference implementation). Grounding: deploy/knowledge/owasp/CheatSheetSeries/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md (implement password strength controls on the server, for every path) and deploy/knowledge/owasp/wstg/document/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/04-Authentication_Testing/07-Testing_for_Weak_Password_Policy.md.
findings.remediation_side_effects: Keeps password reset and change and removes only the weakness: a weak password is refused by the server as the browser already refuses it, a user whose administrator disabled password changes can no longer change one through a method, and a third-party DDP client that called changePassword either gains the REST rules or must switch to the REST route.

findings.title: Integration updates and deletes trust the type the caller names, so one integration permission family reaches the other's objects, script included
findings.category: Broken function-level authorization (type confusion between permission families)
findings.status: CONFIRMED (an account with only the incoming-integration permissions changed and removed an outgoing integration by naming the other type in the body)
findings.confidence_reasoning: Proven by our own run against the pinned build; needs an account, a non-default feature.
findings.known_evidence: Stage 07 F-61: searched integrations.update type webhook-incoming outgoing permission bypass; adjacent only PR #43522 (tests) and issue #13262 (the split permissions).
